children.translated_text: <s>Sāṅkhyasāraḥ</s> (The Essence of Sāṅkhya) / First Part / First Chapter
He who is called <s>Mahat</s> (the Great One), self-born, the sprout of the universe, the Lord,
to that <s>Viṣṇu</s>, the Self of all, the all-conquering one—salutations.
The truth of the Self (<s>ātmatattva</s>) has been briefly elucidated in the <s>Sāṅkhyakārikā</s>;
therefore the discriminative analysis of the essence of <s>Sāṅkhya</s> is elaborated here by <s>Vijñāna</s>[bhikṣu].
The <s>Sāṅkhya</s> method has been mostly compiled in the collection of <s>kārikās</s> (verses);
therefore it is described here briefly, only to the extent of what was left unstated therein.
In the <s>Sāṅkhyabhāṣya</s>, the nature of <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) and the rest has been explained by me at length;

children.text: proktaṃ tasmāt tadapyatra saṅkṣepādeva vakṣyate // ViSs_1,1.4 //
children.translated_text: therefore that too will be stated here only in summary.

children.text: ātmānātmavivekasākṣātkārāt kartṛtvādyakhilābhimānanivṛttyā tatkāryarāgadveṣadharmādharmādyanutpādāt pūrvotpannakarmaṇāṃ cāvidyārāgādisahakāryucchedarūpadānena vipākānārambhakatvāt prārabdhasamāptyanantaraṃ punarjanmābhāvena trividhaduḥkhātyantanivṛttirūpo mokṣo bhavatīti śrutismṛtiḍiṇḍimaḥ / tatra śrutayaḥ / athākāmayamāno yo 'kāmo niṣkāmo na tasya prāṇā utkrāmantīhaiva samavalīyante /

children.translated_text: 'If a person were to know the Self, thinking "I am this,"'
'for what desire and for whose sake would he follow the body?'

Through the direct realization of the discrimination between Self and non-Self, by the cessation of all false identification such as doership and the like, through the non-arising of their effects—attachment, aversion, merit, demerit, etc.—and by rendering previously accumulated <s>karmas</s> incapable of producing results through the cutting off of their auxiliary causes such as ignorance and attachment, after the exhaustion of <s>prārabdha</s> (karma already commenced), <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) in the form of the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering comes about through the absence of rebirth—thus proclaim the <s>Śrutis</s> and <s>Smṛtis</s>. Regarding this, the <s>Śrutis</s> state: 'Now, he who is without desire, who is free from desire, whose desire is fulfilled—his vital breaths (<s>prāṇas</s>) do not depart; right here they are absorbed.'

children.text: yadā sarve pramucyante kāmā ye 'sya hṛdi śritāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'When all the desires that dwell in one's heart are released,'
'then the mortal becomes immortal and attains <s>Brahman</s> here.'
'He who desires objects of desire, thinking of them,'
'is born here and there through his actions;'
'but for one whose desire is fulfilled, whose Self is perfected,'
'all desires dissolve right here.'
'All defects such as attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) are rooted in delusion;'
'the effect of this [delusion] becomes the defect of merit and demerit—thus says the <s>Śruti</s>.'
Such and others are [the <s>Śrutis</s>]. And the <s>Smṛtis</s> such as the <s>Kūrma Purāṇa</s> and others; as stated in the <s>Kūrma Purāṇa</s>:

children.text:
tadvaśādeva sarveṣāṃ sarvadehasamudbhavaḥ /
iti / mokṣadharme ca /

children.translated_text: 'The senses and sense-objects do not approach one who is free from craving;'
'and an embodied being devoid of [sense] organs does not deserve a body again.'
'From that [delusion] alone arises the embodiment in all bodies for all beings.' And in the <s>Mokṣadharma</s>:

children.text:
tasmāt tarṣātmakād rāgād bījājjāyanti jantavaḥ /
iti / nanu rāgābhāve 'pi kevalakarmavaśānnarakādiprāpteḥ kathaṃ rāgasya karmasahakāritvaṃ vipākārambha upapannam / narakādau viśeṣato rāgābhāve 'pi sāmānyato rāgasattvāt / niṣiddhastryādigāmināṃ stryādirāgādeva taptalohamayanārīsamāliṅganādirūpanarakotpatteḥ / yadyapyavidyāsmitārāgadveṣabhayākhyaṃ kleśapañcakameva janmādivipākārambhe karmaṇāṃ sahakāri bhavati /
tadeva saktaḥ saha karmaṇaiti

children.translated_text: [as the <s>Śruti</s> says:] 'The <s>liṅga</s> (subtle body), the mind, wherever one's [consciousness] is poured,'

—since from this <s>Śruti</s> it is established that the general attachment called <s>viṣayavāsanā</s> (impressions of sense objects), born of false identification, desire, aversion, and the like, is itself the auxiliary of <s>karma</s> in producing fruition such as birth;

children.text: yatra yatra mano dehī dhārayet sakalaṃ dhiyā /
children.translated_text: 'Wherever the embodied one fixes the entire mind with concentration,'
'whether from love, hatred, or even fear, one attains that very form.'

'Therefore, beings are born from attachment, which is of the nature of craving, as from a seed.' Now, [one may object:] even in the absence of attachment, since one attains hell and such states through the force of <s>karma</s> alone, how is the auxiliary role of attachment in the commencement of karmic fruition justified? [Reply:] Even in the absence of specific attachment [to hell], attachment in general exists; for those who engage with forbidden women and such, it is precisely from attachment to women etc. that birth in hells characterized by embracing female figures made of heated iron and similar punishments arises. Although the fivefold group of afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) called <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), <s>asmitā</s> (egoism), <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>abhiniveśa</s> (fear of death) collectively serves as the auxiliary of <s>karma</s> in producing fruition such as birth—

children.text:
ityādismṛteśca / tathā ca kleśamūlaḥ karmāśayaḥ / sati mūle tadvipāko jātyāyurbhogā iti yogasūtrābhyāmapyadṛṣṭe tadvipākārambhe ca kleśānāṃ hetutvavacanācca / tathā 'pyavidyāsmitāsattve rāgasyāvaśyakatvāddveṣabhayayośca rāgamūlakatvādrāga eva mukhyato janmādihetutayā yathoktavākyairnirdiśyata iti / nanu /
kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare /
ityādiśruterjñānasya prācīnakarmanāśakatvamevocitaṃ dāhakatvaṃ kathamiṣyata iti cenna /
jñānāgnidagdhakarmāṇaṃ tamāhuḥ paṇḍitaṃ budhāḥ /
ityādivākyairdāhasyāpi śravaṇena lāghavāddāhaparatvasyaiva nāśādivākyeṣvapi kalpanaucityāt / karmaṇāṃ dāhaśca kleśākhyasahakāryucchedena naiṣphalyam / karmaṇāṃ nāśastu prārabdhabhogānte cittanāśādeva bhaviṣyati / ato lokasiddhenāvidyānāśenaiva dvāreṇa karmaphalānutpattisambhavānna jñānasya karmanāśakatvaṃ gauravādityādikaṃ yogavārttike praprañcitamasmābhiriti dik / tasmādvivekasākṣātkārādavidyāsmitārāgādikleśanivṛttau trividhaduḥkhātyantanivṛttirūpaparamapuruṣārthaḥ siddhyatītyupapannam / tathā ca yogasūtradvayam / heyaṃ duḥkhamanāgatam / vivekkhyātiraviplavā hānopāya iti /
children.translated_text: —thus from this and other <s>Smṛtis</s> as well. And so too [from] the two <s>Yoga Sūtras</s>: 'The repository of <s>karma</s> has the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) as its root' and 'When the root exists, its fruition is birth, lifespan, and experience'—since these declare the <s>kleśas</s> to be the cause of both the unseen [karmic force] and the commencement of its fruition. Even so, since <s>rāga</s> (attachment) is indispensable when <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and <s>asmitā</s> (egoism) are present, and since <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion) and <s>abhiniveśa</s> (fear) are rooted in <s>rāga</s>, it is <s>rāga</s> alone that is primarily indicated as the cause of birth and the like by the aforementioned statements. Now, [one may object:] from the <s>Śruti</s> 'His <s>karmas</s> are destroyed when that Supreme, both higher and lower, is seen,' knowledge's capacity to destroy prior <s>karmas</s> is appropriate—how can the capacity to burn [karma] be accepted? [Reply:] This is not so, because from statements like 'The wise call him learned whose <s>karmas</s> have been burned by the fire of knowledge,' since burning is also heard, and due to the elegance [of interpretation], the passages about destruction should also be construed as referring to burning. The 'burning' of <s>karmas</s> means their being rendered fruitless through the cutting off of their auxiliary [cause] called <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). The actual destruction of <s>karmas</s> will occur only through the dissolution of mind (<s>citta</s>) after the experience of <s>prārabdha</s> [karma]. Therefore, since the non-arising of karmic fruits is possible simply through the well-known destruction of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) as the means, knowledge's capacity to destroy <s>karma</s> need not be accepted due to the undue complexity [it would entail]—this and more has been elaborated by us in the <s>Yogavārttika</s>; this is just an indication [of the argument]. Therefore, it is established that through the direct realization of discrimination, when the afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) such as <s>avidyā</s>, <s>asmitā</s>, <s>rāga</s>, etc. cease, the supreme goal of human life (<s>paramapuruṣārtha</s>) in the form of the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering is accomplished. And thus the two <s>Yoga Sūtras</s>: 'The suffering yet to come is to be avoided' and 'Unwavering discriminative discernment (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) is the means of avoidance.'

children.text: iti śrīvijñānabhikṣuviracite sāṅkhyasāre 'bhyarhitattvādādau vivekakhyātiphalasya paramapuruṣārthasya paricchedaḥ // * //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the first chapter on the supreme goal of human life (<s>paramapuruṣārtha</s>), which is the fruit of discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>), in the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> composed by Śrī <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Now, the Second Chapter.

children.text: athātmānātmavivekajñānasya kiṃ svarūpaṃ taducyate / ātmā tāvat sukhaduḥkhādyanubhaviteti sāmānyato lokaprasiddhiḥ anātmā ca prakṛtyādirjaḍavargaḥ tayoranyonyavaidharmyeṇa pariṇāmitvāpariṇāmitvādirūpeṇa doṣaguṇātmakena heyopādeyatayā pṛthaktvena jñānaṃ vivekajñānam / tathā ca śrutiḥ / sa eṣa neti netyātmā 'gṛhyo na hi gṛhyate 'śīryo na hi śīryate 'saṅgo na hi sajyate 'sito na vyathate na riṣyatītyādi / smṛtiśca /

children.translated_text: 'Then he, with senses withdrawn, enlightened by the mirror [of teaching] from the <s>Guru</s>,'
'directly perceived the transformation which, through delusion, had been attributed to himself as belonging to another.'

Now, what is the nature of the knowledge of discrimination between Self and non-Self? That is stated. First, the Self (<s>Ātman</s>) is the experiencer of pleasure, pain, and the like—this is commonly accepted by all. And the non-Self is the insentient category beginning with <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature). The knowledge of their separateness through their mutual differences—in the form of mutability and immutability, etc., characterized by defects and virtues, and as what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted—is discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekajñāna</s>). And thus the <s>Śruti</s>: 'This Self is [described as] "not this, not this" (<s>neti neti</s>)—ungraspable, for it is not grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached, for it does not attach; unfettered, it neither suffers nor is injured,' and so forth. And the <s>Smṛti</s>:
'Then [he realized:] "This <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) is not me, for she is of impure nature;'
'I am of pure and luminous nature"—knowing this, he renounces her.'
'Thus, when the Self is remembered as pure, distinct from the body, senses, and the rest,'
'this entire [<s>Prakṛti</s>] with all her modifications is virtually abandoned, like a snake's [shed] skin.'

children.text: iti / sūtraṃ ca / evaṃ tattvābhyāsānneti netīti tyāgādvivekasiddhiriti / tattvajñānasya lakṣaṇaṃ ca mātsye kṛtam /

children.translated_text: 'When the modification [of <s>Prakṛti</s>] from the <s>Avyakta</s> (unmanifest) at the beginning to the <s>Viśeṣas</s> (particulars) at the end has been described,'
'the knowledge of the difference between the sentient and the insentient is called [true] knowledge.'

And the <s>Sūtra</s> also states: 'Thus, through the practice of truth, by the renunciation [expressed as] "not this, not this" (<s>neti neti</s>), the attainment of discrimination is achieved.' The definition of <s>tattvajñāna</s> (knowledge of reality) has also been given in the <s>Mātsya Purāṇa</s>:

children.text: iti / yadyapyanyonyabhedajñānameva vivekajñānaṃ tathāpyātmaviśeṣyakameva tanmokṣakāraṇaṃ bhavati / ātmā vā 're draṣṭavya ityādi śrutismṛtibhyaḥ / nanvanātmanyātmabuddhirūpā yā 'vidyā pātañjalādiṣūktā tasyāḥ kathamātmaviśeṣyakavivekajñānanāśyatvaṃ prakārādibhedāditi cenna / tādṛśāvidyāyā anātmaviśeṣyakavivekajñānadvāreṇātmaviśeṣyakavivekajñānanāśyatvāditi / yacca yogena nirvikalpakamātmajñānaṃ jāyate tadvivekajñānadvāraiva mokṣakāraṇaṃ bhavati na tu sākṣādavidyānivartakatvābhāvāt / ahaṃ gauraḥ kartā sukhī duḥkhītyādi jñānameva hyavidyā saṃsārānarthahetutayā śrutismṛtinyāyasiddhā tasyāśca nivartikā nāhaṃ gaura ityādirūpā vivekakhyātireva bhavati / samāne viṣaye grāhyābhāvatvaprakārakagrāhyābhāvajñānatvenaiva virodhāt / anyathā śuktanirvikalpakasyāpi idaṃ rajatamiti jñānavirodhitvāpatteḥ / kiñca yatoktābhāvajñāne grāhyajñānavirodhitvasyāvaśyakatayā nirvikalpakajñānasya bhramanivartakatvaṃ na pṛthak kalpyate gauravāt / api cāthā 'ta ādeśo neti neti na hyetasmāditi netyanyat paramastītyādiśrutyā vivekopadeśāpekṣayottamopadeśo nāstītyucyate /

children.translated_text: 'The difference between the field (<s>kṣetra</s>) and the knower of the field (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), thus, with the eye of knowledge,'

children.text: bhūtaprakṛtimokṣaṃ ca ye viduryānti te param //
children.translated_text: 'and the liberation from the <s>Prakṛti</s> (material nature) of beings—those who know this attain the Supreme.'

Although discriminative knowledge is indeed the knowledge of mutual difference, nevertheless it is only [discriminative knowledge] qualified by the Self (<s>ātmaviśeṣyaka</s>) that becomes the cause of liberation—from <s>Śrutis</s> and <s>Smṛtis</s> such as 'The Self indeed is to be seen.' Now, [objection:] how can <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), described in the <s>Pātañjala</s> system and others as the false cognition of the Self in the non-Self, be destroyed by discriminative knowledge qualified by the Self, given the difference of content? [Reply:] This is not so, because such <s>avidyā</s> is destroyed by discriminative knowledge qualified by the Self through the medium of discriminative knowledge qualified by the non-Self. And the direct knowledge of the Self (<s>ātmajñāna</s>) that arises through <s>Yoga</s> as indeterminate (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) cognition becomes the cause of liberation only through the medium of discriminative knowledge, not directly, due to the absence of [direct] capacity to remove <s>avidyā</s>. For <s>avidyā</s>, established by <s>Śruti</s>, <s>Smṛti</s>, and reasoning as the cause of the calamity of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), is precisely the cognition 'I am fair, I am the doer, I am happy, I am unhappy,' and the like; and its remover is none other than discriminative discernment (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) of the form 'I am not fair' and the like, [they being contradictory] precisely as absence-of-apprehensible cognition and apprehensible-absence cognition regarding the same object. Otherwise, even the indeterminate cognition of nacre would absurdly contradict the cognition 'this is silver.' Moreover, since the contradictoriness to erroneous cognition is necessarily [present] in the aforementioned absence-cognition, the capacity of indeterminate cognition to remove error need not be separately postulated, due to undue complexity. Furthermore, from the <s>Śruti</s> 'Now, therefore, the teaching: "not this, not this" (<s>neti neti</s>)—for there is nothing higher than this,' it is stated that there is no instruction superior to the teaching of discrimination—

children.text: iti gītādivākyaiśca vivekajñānasyaiva mokṣahetutvamucyate / ato vivekajñānameva sākṣādavidyānivṛttyā mokṣahetuḥ / yogena kevalātmasākṣātkārastu yogyānupalabdhividhayopādhyādigatadharmābhāvamupādhyādibhedaṃ ca grāhayati tato 'vidyānivṛttiriti / etena sarvabhūteṣu samatājñānamātmanaḥ sarvātmakatvādijñānaṃ ca śrutismṛtyorgīyamānaṃ vivekajñānasyaiva śeṣabhūtaṃ sarvadarśaneṣu mantavyam / jñānāntarāṇāṃ sākṣādabhimānānivartakatvāt / brahmamīmāṃsāyāṃ tvayaṃ viśeṣo yat paramātmavivekaśeṣatvam / sāṅkhyaśāstre tu sāmānyātmavivekaśeṣatvamiti dik / nanu yathoktavivekakhyātito 'pyatyantamavidyocchedo na ghaṭate / vivekakhyāteravidyāpratibandhakatvamātratvena vivekakhyātināśottaraṃ punarabhimānasambhavāt / śuktirajatavivekadarśino 'pi kālāntare śuktau rajatabhramavaditi / maivam / dṛṣṭāntavaiṣamyāt / śuktyādiṣu jāte 'pi sākṣātkāre dūratvādirūpaviṣayadoṣāṇāṃ paṭalādirūpakaraṇadoṣāṇāṃ cotpattisambhavena punarbhramo yuktaḥ / anātmanyātmābhimāne tvanādivāsanaiva doṣaḥ sarvāstikasammataḥ jātamātrasyābhimāne doṣāntarānupalabdheḥ / sā mithyājñānavāsanā yadā vivekakhyātiparamparājanyadṛḍhavāsanonmūlitā tadaiva vivekasākṣātkāraniṣṭhocyate / tatpūrvamavaśyaṃ vāsanāleśato mithyāṃśasya kasyāpyātmani bhāvāt tasyāṃ ca vivekakhyātiniṣṭhāyāṃ jātāyāṃ na punarabhimānaḥ sambhavati vāsanākhyadoṣābhāvāditi tu mahadvaiṣamyam / yadi tu buddhipuruṣayoranyonyapratibimbanādikamavivekakāraṇaṃ doṣa iṣyate tadā tu taddoṣaṃ bādhitvaiva vivekasākṣātkāra udita iti na tasya punarbhramahetutvaṃ phalabalena yogajadharmāsahakṛtasyaiva tasya doṣatvakalpanāsambhavāditi / vivekakhyātiniṣṭhā ca gītādiṣu lakṣitā /
prakāśaṃ ca pravṛttiṃ ca mohameva ca pāṇḍava /
children.translated_text: O <s>Pāṇḍava</s>, illumination, activity, and delusion —

children.text: na dveṣṭi sampravṛttāni na nivṛttāni kāṅkṣati //
children.translated_text: he neither hates them when they arise, nor longs for them when they cease.

Thus, by statements of the <s>Gītā</s> and other texts, it is declared that <s>vivekajñāna</s> (discriminative knowledge) alone is the cause of <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation). Therefore, <s>vivekajñāna</s> alone is the direct cause of liberation through the removal of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). The direct realization of the pure self through <s>yoga</s>, by the method of non-apprehension of fitness, makes one apprehend the absence of attributes belonging to the limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) and the distinction from the limiting adjuncts, and from that follows the removal of ignorance. By this, the knowledge of equality toward all beings, the knowledge of the self being the self of all, and similar knowledge celebrated in <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s>, should be understood in all philosophical systems as subsidiary to discriminative knowledge alone, because other forms of knowledge do not directly remove false identification (<s>abhimāna</s>). In <s>Brahma-mīmāṃsā</s>, however, the distinction is that they are subsidiary to the discrimination of the supreme self (<s>Paramātman</s>); in <s>Sāṃkhya</s> teaching, they are subsidiary to the discrimination of the self in general — this is the direction. Objection: Even from the aforementioned <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative discernment), the complete destruction of ignorance does not occur, because discriminative discernment merely obstructs ignorance, and after the destruction of discriminative discernment, false identification can arise again — just as even one who has discerned the distinction between shell and silver can, at a later time, again have the illusion of silver in a shell. Reply: This is not so, because of the dissimilarity of the example. In the case of shell etc., even after direct perception has arisen, repeated error is reasonable because of the possibility of object-defects such as distance and instrument-defects such as cataracts arising again. But in the false identification of the self in the non-self, beginningless latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) alone is the defect, as accepted by all theists, since no other defect is found for the false identification present from birth. When that latent impression of false knowledge is uprooted by the firm impression born of a continuous series of discriminative discernments, only then is it called the culmination of the direct realization of discrimination. Before that, necessarily, due to a trace of latent impression, some element of falsity remains in the self. And when that culmination of discriminative discernment has arisen, false identification does not occur again, due to the absence of the defect called latent impression — this is the great dissimilarity from the shell-silver example. If, however, the mutual reflection between <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (consciousness) and similar factors are accepted as the defect causing non-discrimination, then the direct realization of discrimination has arisen only after sublating that defect, so it cannot be the cause of repeated error, because it is impossible to attribute the status of defect to that which lacks the cooperation of <s>yoga</s>-born <s>dharma</s>, by the force of its result. And the culmination of discriminative discernment is indicated in the <s>Gītā</s> and other texts:
He who sits as if indifferent, who is not shaken by the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities),
who has renounced the undertaking of all actions — he is said to have transcended the <s>guṇas</s>.

children.text: iti / guṇātīto nivṛttaguṇābhimānaḥ / adhikaṃ tu jñānilakṣaṇamagre vakṣyāmaḥ / nanvevamapi vivekapratiyogipadārthānāmānantyena prātisvikarūpaiḥ sarvapadārthebhyo vivekagrahāsambhavāt kathaṃ vivekakhyātermokṣahetutvamiti cenna / dṛśyatvapariṇāmitvādisāmānyarūpairvivekagrahasambhavāt / tathā hi / draṣṭā svasākṣātprakāśebhyo bhinnaḥ prakāśakatvādyo yasya prakāśakaḥ sa tasmādbhinnaḥ yathā ghaṭādāloko vṛttiprakāśyācca vṛttirityanumānenādāvantardṛśyebhyo buddhivṛttitadārūḍhārthebhyo vivekato buddhīsākṣī sidhyati / karmakartṛvirodhaścānukūlastarkaḥ / atra ātmani vyabhicāravāraṇāya sākṣātpadam / vṛttidvāraivātmanaḥ svaviṣayatvāt / nanvatrānumāne buddhivṛttimātrādvivekaḥ sidhyatu / tasyā eva sākṣadātmadṛśyatvāt na prakṛtyādibhya iti cenna / vṛttīnāmajñātasattvābhāvena hyatrānumāne lāghavādvakṣyamāṇatarkagaṇāccākhilavṛttīnāṃ draṣṭā vibhukūṭasthanityaikajñānasvarūpatayaiva sidhyati / yathā naiyāyikānāṃ kṣitiḥ sakartṛkā kāryatvādityanumāne lāghavāt karturekatvanityatvādikaṃ tadvat / tatra vibhutvaṃ paricchinnabhinnatvaṃ kūṭasthatvādikatvaṃ ca pariṇāmibhinnatvādikamato buddhyātmanordṛgdṛśyarūpato vivekagrahe sati taduttarānumānena pariṇāmitvāpariṇāmitvādirūpaiḥ sāmānyato 'pyātmānātmavivekagraho ghaṭata iti / ataeva pātañjale sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātireva mokṣahetutayā sthale sthale vyāsabhāṣye proktā / sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātirūpadṛgdṛśyavivekagrahottaraṃ yathoktarītyā prakṛtyādivivekagrahāt / tatra ca sattvaśabde buddhisthatvena buddhisattvamuktamiti / evaṃ ca prakṛtyādipadārthānāṃ viśiṣyajñānābhāve 'pi tadvivekajñānaṃ ghaṭate / etena dṛgdṛśyavivekādavidyānivṛttiriti prācāṃ pravādo 'pyupapāditaḥ / kiñcātmā prakṛtitatkāryebhyo bhinno 'pariṇāmitvādityādyanumānairapi sāmānyato dṛśyaviveko draṣṭari sambhavatīti / yattvādhunikā vedāntibruvā dṛśyatvenaiva prakṛtyādīnāṃ draṣṭṛtvena ca prakṛtyādyakhilajaḍebhya ātmavivekaṃ manyante /
ghaṭadraṣṭā ghaṭādbhinnaḥ sarvathā na ghaṭo yathā /
children.translated_text: Just as the seer of a pot is entirely different from the pot and is in no way the pot,
so too the seer of the body is different from the body — in the form 'I am not this' and so forth —

Thus, one who has transcended the <s>guṇas</s> is one whose false identification with the <s>guṇas</s> has ceased. But we shall state the additional characteristics of the knower further on. Objection: Even so, since the counter-correlates of discrimination are infinite in number, and grasping discrimination from all entities through their individual forms is impossible, how can <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative discernment) be the cause of <s>mokṣa</s>? Reply: This is not so, because it is possible to grasp discrimination through general characteristics such as <s>dṛśyatva</s> (being an object of perception) and <s>pariṇāmitva</s> (being subject to transformation). For instance: the seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) is different from those that are directly illuminated by him, because he is the illuminator — whatever illuminates something is different from it, just as a lamp from a pot. And a mental modification (<s>vṛtti</s>) is illuminated by that which illuminates modifications — by this inference, first, through discrimination from internal objects, namely mental modifications and objects superimposed upon them, the witness (<s>sākṣin</s>) of the intellect is established. And the contradiction between object and agent is a supporting argument. Here, the word 'directly' is to prevent deviation in the case of the self, since the self becomes its own object only through mental modifications. Objection: In this inference, let discrimination be established only from mental modifications, since only they are directly objects of the self, not from <s>Prakṛti</s> etc. Reply: This is not so, because in this inference, since there are no mental modifications whose existence is unknown, by parsimony and from the group of arguments to be stated, the seer of all modifications is established as having the nature of a single, all-pervading, immutable, eternal consciousness alone — just as for the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>, in the inference that the earth has a maker because it is an effect, by parsimony the unity, eternality, etc. of the maker are established. Here, all-pervasiveness is difference from the limited, immutability and so forth are difference from the transformable — therefore, when discrimination in the form of seer and seen between <s>buddhi</s> and <s>ātman</s> is grasped, subsequently through inference, discrimination of self from non-self through general characteristics such as being subject to transformation versus not being subject to transformation is also possible. Therefore, in the <s>Pātañjala</s> system, the discernment of the difference between <s>sattva</s> (purity of intellect) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (consciousness) alone is stated everywhere in the <s>Vyāsa-bhāṣya</s> as the cause of liberation. The discernment of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> enables the grasping of discrimination from <s>Prakṛti</s> etc. in the manner described, following the grasping of the seer-seen distinction. And there, by the word <s>sattva</s>, <s>buddhi-sattva</s> (the purity of the intellect) is meant, since it pertains to the intellect. Thus, even without specific knowledge of individual entities such as <s>Prakṛti</s>, discriminative knowledge regarding them is possible. By this, the doctrine of the ancients that the removal of <s>avidyā</s> comes from the discrimination of seer and seen is also justified. Moreover, through inferences such as 'the self is different from <s>Prakṛti</s> and its effects because it is not subject to transformation,' discrimination from the visible is possible in the seer even through general characteristics. However, those modern self-styled <s>Vedāntins</s> who hold that the discrimination of the self from <s>Prakṛti</s> and all other insentient entities is merely through their being objects of perception and the self being the seer —

children.text: tanna / ātmā vā 're draṣṭavya ityādiśrutibhirātmano 'pi dṛśyatvāt sākṣāddṛśyatvavivakṣayā ca prakṛtyāderasaṅgrahāt karaṇadvāraiva taddarśanāt / athaivaṃ kalpanīyaṃ ātmano vṛttivyāpyatvameva dṛśyatvaṃ śrutyādibhirvidhīyate na tu prakāśyatvarūpaphalavyāpyatvam / svayamprakāśasvarūpasya prakāśāpekṣāvirahāt / ato 'tra dṛśyatvaṃ prakāśyatvaṃ taccātmani nāstīti tadapi tuccham / yathā hyahamityanubhūyamāno 'pyātmā caitanyākhyaphalavyāpyo na bhavatīti bhavadbhirucyate tathaiva bauddhairapīṣyate sukhaduḥkhādimattvenāpi buddhiḥ svaprakāśatayā caitanyavyāpyā na bhavatīti / tathā cātmanīva buddhāvapi dṛśyatvāsiddhyā dṛśyatvena rūpeṇa buddhiviveko 'tyantāpekṣito 'pi na sidhyatīti bhāṣyādiṣu cānyānyatra dūṣaṇānyuktānīti dik / nanu sambhavatyevaṃ sāmānyarūpeṇa vivekagrahaḥ / tathāpi sāmānyānyeva bahūni santi pariṇāmitvasaṃhatyakāritvasukhaduḥkhamohātmakatvacaturviṃśatitattvatvādīnyatastaistai rūpairvivekagrahāṇāṃ mokṣahetutve 'nanugamadoṣa iti cenna / abhimānapratibandhakajñānatvenaivānugamāditi / athaivaṃ sāmānyarūpeṇa vivekasyaiva sarvābhimānanivartakatayā nāhaṃ deho nendriyāṇityādipratyekarūpairvivekagrahāṇāṃ mokṣahetutvaṃ śrutismṛtyorucyamānaṃ kathaṃ ghaṭeteti cenna / avāntaravivekānāṃ sāmānyavivekaprapañcamātratvāditi //
children.translated_text: that is not correct, because the self too is an object of perception according to <s>śruti</s> texts such as 'the self indeed is to be seen,' and because <s>Prakṛti</s> etc. are not included in what is intended by direct objectness of perception, since they are perceived only through instruments. If it be argued that what should be understood is: the objectness of the self, as taught by <s>śruti</s> etc., is only being pervaded by mental modifications (<s>vṛtti</s>), not being pervaded by the result in the form of being illuminated — since a self-luminous entity has no need for illumination — therefore, objectness here means being illuminated, and that does not exist in the self — that too is worthless. For just as you say that the self, though experienced as 'I,' is not pervaded by the result called consciousness, so too the <s>Bauddhas</s> (Buddhists) hold that the intellect, even though possessing pleasure, pain, etc., being self-luminous, is not pervaded by consciousness. And thus, since objectness of perception is not established even in the intellect just as in the self, the discrimination of the intellect through the characteristic of objectness, though greatly desired, is not established either — and in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> and other texts, various other refutations are stated elsewhere — this is the direction. Objection: Granted that discrimination through general characteristics is thus possible; nevertheless, there are many general characteristics — being subject to transformation, being produced by aggregation, having the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, being the twenty-four <s>tattvas</s> (principles) — and so, if discriminations through these various forms are each the cause of <s>mokṣa</s>, there would be the fault of lacking a unifying principle. Reply: This is not so, because the unifying factor is being the knowledge that counteracts false identification (<s>abhimāna</s>). Objection: If discrimination through general characteristics alone removes all false identification, how can the scriptures (<s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s>) teach that discriminations through specific forms such as 'I am not the body,' 'not the senses,' etc. are the cause of liberation? Reply: This is not so, because the subsidiary discriminations are merely elaborations of the general discrimination.

children.text: iti śrīvijñānabhikṣuviracite sāṅkhyasāre mokṣahetuvivekajñānasya svarūpasya paricchedaḥ // * //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the chapter on the nature of <s>vivekajñāna</s> (discriminative knowledge) as the cause of <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), in the <s>Sāṃkhyasāra</s> composed by <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Now begins the third chapter.

children.text: atha ke te prakṛtyādayo yebhyaḥ puruṣo vivecanīya ityucyate /
children.translated_text: Now, what are those entities such as <s>Prakṛti</s> etc. from which <s>Puruṣa</s> (consciousness) is to be discriminated? It is stated:

<s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-principle), the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements), the eleven <s>indriyas</s> (sense organs and organs of action plus mind),
and the five gross elements — these, in general, are indeed twenty-four.

children.text: eteṣveva dharmadharmyabhedena guṇakarmasāmānyānāmantarbhāvaḥ / tatra prakṛtitvaṃ sākṣāt paramparayā 'khilavikāropādānatvaṃ prakṛṣṭākṛtiḥ pariṇāmarūpā 'syā iti vyutpatteḥ / prakṛtiḥ śaktirajā pradhānamavyaktaṃ tamo māyā 'vidyetyādayaḥ prakṛteḥ paryāyāḥ /
brāhmīti vidyā 'vidyeti māyeti ca tathā pare /
children.translated_text: <s>Brāhmī</s>, <s>Vidyā</s> (knowledge), <s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance), <s>Māyā</s> (illusion), and likewise others,
<s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Parā</s> (the supreme) — thus declare the great sages.

Among these alone, through the distinction of property and property-bearer, the general categories of <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) and <s>karmas</s> (actions) are included. Here, <s>prakṛtitva</s> (the nature of being Prakṛti) means being the material cause of all modifications, either directly or indirectly, from the etymology: 'she whose distinguished form (<s>prakṛṣṭā ākṛtiḥ</s>), which is transformation, belongs to her.' <s>Prakṛti</s>, <s>Śakti</s> (power), <s>Rajā</s>, <s>Pradhāna</s> (the principal), <s>Avyakta</s> (the unmanifest), <s>Tamas</s> (darkness), <s>Māyā</s> (illusion), <s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance), and others are synonyms of <s>Prakṛti</s>.

iti smṛteḥ / sā ca sāmyāvasthayopalakṣitaṃ sattvādidravyatrayam / kāryasattvādivāraṇāyopalakṣitāntam / sāmyāvasthā ca nyūnādhikabhāvenāsaṃhananāvasthā akāryāvastheti yāvat / mahadādikaṃ tu kāryasattvādikaṃ na kadā 'pyakāryāvasthaṃ bhavatīti tadvyāvṛttiḥ / vaiṣamyāvasthāyāmapi prakṛtitvasiddhaya upalakṣitamityuktam / akāryamiti tūpalakṣitāntasya niṣkṛṣṭārthaḥ / sattvādiguṇavatī sattvādyatiriktā prakṛtiriti na śaṅkanīyam / sattvādīnāmataddharmatvaṃ tadrūpatvāditi sāṅkhyasūtreṇa sattvādīnāṃ prakṛtisvarūpahetunā prakṛtidharmatvapratiṣedhāt / yogasūtratadbhāṣyābhyāmapi guṇānāmeva prakṛtitvavacanācca / guṇebhya eva kāryotpattau tadanyaprakṛtikalpanāvaiyarthyācca / prakṛterguṇā ityādivākyaṃ tu vanasya vṛkṣā itivad bodhyam /

guṇāntaravyāvṛttaprakāśādiphalopahitaḥ sattvādivyavahārayogyaḥ pariṇāma iti / etenāṣṭāviṃśatitattvapakṣo 'pyupapādito mantavyaḥ / vaiṣamya eva sattvādivyavahāraśca śrutau dṛśyate / yathā tama saṃyogavibhāgādimattayā 'nāśritatvopādānatvādinā ca draṣṭavye 'pi puruṣopakaraṇatvāt puruṣabandhakatvācca guṇaśabdenocyate / indriyādivat / guṇānāṃ sukhaduḥkhamohātmakatvapravādastu sattvamuttamatvamiti vyutpattyā hi dharmaprādhānyenottamaṃ puruṣopakaraṇaṃ sattvaśabdārthaḥ / madhyamaṃ ca rajaḥśabdārtho rāgayogāt / adhamaṃ ca tamaḥśabdārthaḥ / adharmāvaraṇayogāt / tāni ca vaidharmyam / evaṃ calatvādinā gurutvādinā ca bahūnāṃ rajasāṃ bahūnāṃ ca tamasāṃ tadubhayamuktamiti / kiñca yadi sattvāditrayamekaikavyaktireva syāt tat trayaṃ vibhveva vaktavyam / ekadā children.translated_text:
Thus from the <s>Smṛti</s>. And that (<s>Prakṛti</s>) is the triad of substances beginning with <s>sattva</s>, characterized by the state of equilibrium. The term 'characterized' is used to exclude the product-<s>sattva</s> etc. The state of equilibrium is the state of non-combination through excess or deficiency—that is, the state of non-productiveness. But <s>Mahat</s> and the rest, being products of <s>sattva</s> etc., never exist in a non-productive state—thus they are distinguished from <s>Prakṛti</s>. It is said that 'characterized' is used to establish the nature of <s>Prakṛti</s> even in the state of disequilibrium. 'Non-product' is the extracted meaning of the characterizing term. One should not suspect that <s>Prakṛti</s> possesses the qualities of <s>sattva</s> etc. and is something different from <s>sattva</s> etc. Because the <s>Sāṃkhya Sūtra</s>—'<s>sattva</s> etc. do not have its properties because they are of its very nature'—denies that <s>sattva</s> etc. are properties of <s>Prakṛti</s> on the ground that they constitute <s>Prakṛti</s>'s own essential nature. And because the <s>Yoga Sūtra</s> and its commentary also state that the <s>guṇas</s> themselves are <s>Prakṛti</s>. And because when products arise from the <s>guṇas</s> alone, postulating a <s>Prakṛti</s> different from them would be futile. But statements like 'the <s>guṇas</s> of <s>Prakṛti</s>' should be understood like 'the trees of the forest.'
'<s>Sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>—these are the <s>guṇas</s> that arose from <s>Prakṛti</s>.'
This statement about <s>sattva</s> etc. being products of <s>Prakṛti</s>, being in conflict with statements about the eternality of the <s>guṇas</s>, pertains only to the product-<s>sattva</s> etc. that have become the cause of <s>Mahat-tattva</s>. For the creation of <s>Mahat</s> etc. is heard to arise from the disequilibrium of the <s>guṇas</s>. And that disequilibrium is a transformation through the strengthening of the same type, endowed with results such as illumination etc. distinguished from the other <s>guṇas</s>, suitable for designation as <s>sattva</s> etc. By this, the doctrine of twenty-eight principles should also be considered established. The designation of <s>sattva</s> etc. in the state of disequilibrium alone is seen in the <s>Śruti</s>: 'As indeed this was <s>tamas</s> alone in the beginning; that, impelled by the Supreme, attained disequilibrium—that indeed is the form of <s>rajas</s>; that, indeed impelled, attained disequilibrium—that indeed is the form of <s>sattva</s>.' And the triad of <s>sattva</s> etc., though possessing qualities like pleasure, illumination, lightness, clarity etc., and possessing conjunction, disjunction etc., and though they should be seen as substances due to being independent substrates and material causes etc., are called by the word '<s>guṇa</s>' because they serve <s>Puruṣa</s> and because they bind <s>Puruṣa</s>—like the senses etc. The statement that the <s>guṇas</s> are of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is because there is no difference between property and property-bearer—like the mind being of the nature of resolve. Among these, <s>sattva</s>, though having many properties like pleasure, clarity, illumination etc., is predominantly said to be of the nature of pleasure. Similarly, <s>rajas</s>, though having many properties like pain, turbidity, activity etc., is predominantly said to be of the nature of pain. Likewise, <s>tamas</s>, though having many properties like delusion, concealment, inertia etc., is predominantly said to be of the nature of delusion. Those very properties become their defining characteristics. And the names <s>sattva</s> etc. are etymologically meaningful. For by the derivation '<s>sattva</s> means the state of being, i.e., excellence,' the meaning of the word <s>sattva</s> is: the best instrument for <s>Puruṣa</s> by predominance of virtue. The meaning of the word <s>rajas</s> is the middling instrument, because of association with passion. The meaning of the word <s>tamas</s> is the lowest instrument, because of association with vice and concealment. And those <s>sattva</s> etc. each have innumerable instances. From the <s>Sāṃkhya Sūtra</s>: 'The <s>guṇas</s> have mutual similarity and dissimilarity through properties like lightness etc.' For in this <s>sūtra</s>, by lightness etc., many <s>sattvas</s> have similarity among themselves and by the same properties, dissimilarity from <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>. Similarly, by mobility etc. and heaviness etc., both similarity and dissimilarity of many <s>rajases</s> and many <s>tamases</s> are stated. Moreover, if the triad of <s>sattva</s> etc. were each a single instance, then those three would have to be said to be all-pervading, because it is heard that multiple universes etc. are created simultaneously. And thus the infinite variety of products would not be possible. Nor can it be said that variety comes from variety of combinations, because for three all-pervading <s>guṇas</s>, variety of combination is inherently impossible, and because there is no other substance that could serve as a delimiter. Therefore, <s>sattva</s> etc. are substances with innumerable instances. The statement of their being three is through the three delimiting conditions of <s>sattva</s>-ness etc., like the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> statement of nine substances—this is established. And those <s>sattva</s> etc. have atomic, all-pervading, and medium dimensions as appropriate. Otherwise there would be contradiction with the statement that <s>rajas</s> has a mobile nature. And because all-pervasiveness is appropriate for being the cause of <s>ākāśa</s> (space). And because if all causal substances were all-pervading, the limited nature of products would be inexplicable. If one objects that this amounts to saying that the earthly atoms etc. stated by the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> are themselves <s>Prakṛti</s>—no, because of our distinctive position that the causal substances lack qualities like smell etc., and hence earth-ness etc. does not exist in them. This has been stated in the <s>Viṣṇu Purāṇa</s> etc.:
That unmanifest cause which is called <s>Pradhāna</s> by the best of sages,
is declared to be the subtle <s>Prakṛti</s>, eternal, of the nature of both being and non-being.
It is devoid of sound and touch, unconnected with form and the rest,
possessed of three <s>guṇas</s>, the womb of the world, without beginning, the source and dissolution of all.

children.text:
ityādinā /
vaiśeṣikāṇāṃ kāraṇadravyeṣu gandhādyanumānaṃ tu bhāṣye 'smābhirnirākṛtam / athaivamapi prakṛteraṇuvibhusādhāraṇasattvādyanekavyaktirupatve 'paricchinnatvaikatvākriyatvasiddhāntakṣatiriti maivam / kāraṇadravyatvarūpaprakṛtitvenaivāparicchinnatvavacanāt / gandhatvena gandhānāṃ pṛthivīvyāpakatāvat / ākāśādiprakṛtīnāṃ vibhutvenaiva prakṛtivibhutvasiddhāntopapatteśca / tathā puruṣabhedena sargabhedena ca bhedābhāvasyaivaikaśabdārthatvāt / ajāmekāmiti śrutitastathā 'vagamāt / athādhyavasāyābhimānādikriyārāhityasyaivākriyaśabdārthatvāt / anyathā śrutismṛtiṣūktasya prakṛtikṣobhasyānupapatteriti / prakṛtigatāścāpare viśeṣā bhāṣye draṣṭavyāḥ / prakṛtyanumānaṃ cedam / sukhaduḥkhamohātmakaṃ mahadādikāryaṃ sukhaduḥkhamohātmakadravyakāryaṃ sukhaduḥkhamohātmakatvāt vastrādikāryaśayyādivaditi / śrutismṛtī cātrānugrāhakastarkaḥ / evaṃ sāmānyato 'numitāyāḥ prakṛterviśeṣāḥ śāstrādyogāccāvagantavyāḥ / anumānasya sāmānyamātraviṣayakatvāt / nanvantareva sukhādikamupalabhyate bāhyavastuṣu sukhādau kiṃ pramāṇaṃ yena dṛṣṭāntatā syāditi / ucyate / antaḥkaraṇasya sukhādihetutayā viṣayeṣu sukhādikaṃ sidhyati / na ca rūpādigatottamatvādikameva sukhādyutpādane niyāmakam / uttamatvāderjātirūpatve nīlatvapītatvādinā jātisāṅkaryāpatteḥ / kālādibhedairekasyā eva rūpavyakteḥ sukhaduḥkhotpādakatvācca / ataḥ sukhādimattvamevottamatvādikam / kiñca ghaṭarūpamiti pratyayavat strīsukhaṃ candanasukhamityādipratyayādapi viṣaye sukhādyucitam / adhikaṃ tu bhāṣye draṣṭavyam / tadevaṃ prakṛtirnirūpitā / mahattattvaṃ nirūpyate / prakṛteḥ sakāśādbuddhyākhyaṃ mahattattvaṃ jāyate / tasya dharmādirūpaprakṛṣṭaguṇayogān mahatsañjñā tadeva ca lakṣaṇam / mahān buddhiḥ prajñetyādayaśca tasya paryāyāḥ / tathā coktamanugītāyām /

children.translated_text: The Great, the Self, Intelligence, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Jiṣṇu</s>, the auspicious and powerful <s>Śambhu</s>,

children.text: buddhiḥ prajñopalabdhiśca tathā brahmā dhṛtiḥ smṛtiḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect), <s>Prajñā</s> (wisdom), <s>Upalabdhi</s> (apprehension), and also <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Dhṛti</s> (steadfastness), <s>Smṛti</s> (memory)—

By such statements etc.
The <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> inference of smell etc. in causal substances has been refuted by us in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. If one objects that even so, if <s>Prakṛti</s> has multiple instances of <s>sattva</s> etc. of atomic, all-pervading, and medium dimensions, the doctrines of its being unlimited, one, and inactive are violated—this is not so. Because the statement of unlimitedness is only with respect to <s>Prakṛti</s>-hood in the form of being a causal substance—like the pervasion of all smells by smell-ness as earth pervades odors. And because the doctrine of <s>Prakṛti</s>'s all-pervasiveness is established through the all-pervasiveness of the <s>Prakṛtis</s> of <s>ākāśa</s> etc. alone. Similarly, because the meaning of the word 'one' is the absence of division by differences in <s>Puruṣa</s> or by differences in creation—because this is understood from the <s>Śruti</s> 'the one unborn.' And because the meaning of the word 'inactive' is only the absence of activities like determination, ego-sense etc.—otherwise the agitation of <s>Prakṛti</s> stated in <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s> would be inexplicable. Other specific details regarding <s>Prakṛti</s> should be seen in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. And the inference of <s>Prakṛti</s> is as follows: the products beginning with <s>Mahat</s>, being of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, are products of a substance of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because they are of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion—like cloth etc. being products of thread, bed etc. <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>, along with reasoning, support this. The specific features of <s>Prakṛti</s>, thus generally inferred, are to be understood from scripture etc., because inference has only generalities as its object. If one asks: pleasure etc. are perceived only internally; what is the evidence for pleasure etc. in external objects, by which they could serve as examples? It is replied: through the internal organ being the cause of pleasure etc., pleasure etc. are established in objects. Nor is the excellence etc. residing in form etc. alone the determining factor in producing pleasure etc., because if excellence etc. were universals, there would be the absurdity of mixture of universals with blue-ness, yellow-ness etc., and because one and the same instance of form produces both pleasure and pain through differences of time etc. Therefore, excellence etc. is nothing other than possessing pleasure etc. Moreover, just as cognitions like 'the form of a pot' attribute form to objects, from cognitions like 'the pleasure of a woman,' 'the pleasure of sandal' etc., pleasure etc. are appropriate in objects. Further details should be seen in the <s>Bhāṣya</s>. Thus <s>Prakṛti</s> has been described. <s>Mahat-tattva</s> (the Great Principle) is now described. From <s>Prakṛti</s> arises the <s>Mahat-tattva</s> called <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect). Its designation as 'Mahat' (the Great) is due to its connection with excellent qualities in the form of <s>dharma</s> etc., and that itself is its definition. 'Mahān,' '<s>Buddhi</s>,' '<s>Prajñā</s>' etc. are its synonyms. And thus it is said in the <s>Anugītā</s>:
by these synonymous terms, the Great Self is spoken of.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,

children.text: sarvataḥ śrutimāṃlloke sarvaṃ vyāpya sa tiṣṭhati /
children.translated_text: with ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all.
<s>Aṇimā</s> (minuteness), <s>Laghimā</s> (lightness), attainment, lordship, splendor, and imperishability—
those who possess knowledge, who are ungreedy, who have conquered anger,
all these, being liberated, attain greatness.
<s>Viṣṇu</s> alone becomes the self-born Lord in the primal creations.

children.text:
iti / atra sattvādyaṃśatrayeṇa mahato devatātrayopādhitvāt tadavivekena brahmaviṣṇuśivatvavacanam / taduktaṃ viṣṇau /
sāttviko rājasaścaiva tāmasaśca tridhā mahān /
iti / mātsye ca /

children.translated_text: From <s>Pradhāna</s> with its modifications, <s>Mahat-tattva</s> was born,
because the awareness called 'great' always arises in the worlds.

Thus. Here, because the three portions of <s>sattva</s> etc. in <s>Mahat</s> serve as the limiting adjuncts for the three deities, they are spoken of as <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, and <s>Śiva</s> without distinction. This is stated in the <s>Viṣṇu Purāṇa</s>: 'The <s>Mahat</s> is threefold: <s>sāttvika</s>, <s>rājasa</s>, and <s>tāmasa</s>.' And in the <s>Mātsya Purāṇa</s>:
From the agitated <s>guṇas</s>, three deities were born:
one form, three deities—<s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, and <s>Maheśvara</s>.

children.text: iti / aṇimetyādibhāvanirdeśo dharmadharmyabhedāt / brahmaśaṅkarāpekṣayā 'pyādau viṣṇurūpeṇaiva mahānāvirbhavatīti viṣṇurevetyardhenoktam / ekameva mahattattvamaṃśato rajastamaḥsambhedena pariṇataṃ sad vyaṣṭijīvānāmupādhiradharmādiyuktaṃ kṣudramapi bhavati / mahaduparāgādviparītamiti sāṅkhyasūtrāt / mahattattvasya prādhānyenāsādhāraṇyena cādhyavasāyo vṛttiḥ / mahadahaṅkāramanastritayātmakasyāntaḥkaraṇasya mahattattvaṃ bījāvastheti / atra prakṛtermahān mahato 'haṅkāra ityādisṛṣṭikrame śāstrameva pramāṇam / anumānena sāmānyataḥ kāryāṇāṃ sakāraṇakatvamātrasiddheḥ na tu sṛṣṭau bhūtādikramo vā 'ntaḥkaraṇādikramo vetyekataravadhārakamanumānaṃ sambhavati / spaṣṭaliṅgābhāvāt / śrutismṛtyanugṛhītaṃ yathākathañcilliṅgaṃ tu mahadādikrame 'stīti bhāṣye 'smābhiḥ pradarśitam / mahattattvaṃ nirūpitam / ahaṅkāro nirūpyate / mahattattvādahaṅkāra utpadyate / aṅkurāt śākhāvat / tasya cābhimānavṛttikatvādahaṅkārasañjñā / kumbhakārasañjñāvat / tadeva lakṣaṇam / tasya ca paryāyāḥ kaurme proktāḥ /

children.translated_text: <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), <s>abhimāna</s> (self-attribution), <s>kartā</s> (agent), and <s>mantā</s> (thinker)—thus it is remembered,

children.text: ātmā ca prakulo jīvo yataḥ sarvāḥ pravṛttayaḥ //
children.translated_text: as well as <s>ātman</s> (self), <s>prakula</s> (progenitor), and <s>jīva</s> (individual soul), from which all activities proceed.

Thus. The indication of attributes such as <s>aṇimā</s> (atomic minuteness) and others is due to the non-difference of property and property-bearer. Even in relation to <s>Brahmā</s> and <s>Śaṅkara</s>, it is said in the half-verse 'it is <s>Viṣṇu</s> alone' because <s>Mahat</s> (the Great Principle) first manifests in the form of <s>Viṣṇu</s>. The one <s>Mahat-tattva</s> (Great Principle) alone, when partially transformed through admixture of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, becomes the limiting adjunct of individual souls, endowed with <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness) and such, and can also become diminished. From the <s>Sāṅkhya-sūtra</s>: 'the opposite due to the influence of <s>Mahat</s>.' The function of <s>Mahat-tattva</s> is primarily and uniquely determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>). The <s>Mahat-tattva</s> is the seed-state of the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (inner instrument) which consists of the triad of <s>Mahat</s>, <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>, and <s>Manas</s>. Here, regarding the order of creation—'from <s>Prakṛti</s> arises <s>Mahat</s>, from <s>Mahat</s> arises <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>'—scripture alone is the authority. Through inference, only the general fact that effects have causes can be established, but no inference can determine whether in creation the order is that of elements or that of the inner instruments, due to the absence of a clear inferential mark. However, we have shown in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> that there is some kind of inferential mark, supported by <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>, for the order beginning with <s>Mahat</s>. The <s>Mahat-tattva</s> has been examined. Now <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-principle) is examined. From the <s>Mahat-tattva</s>, <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> is produced, like a branch from a sprout. It is called <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> because its function is self-attribution (<s>abhimāna</s>), just as a potter is named after his function. That itself is its definition. Its synonyms are stated in the <s>Kūrma Purāṇa</s>:

children.text: iti / sa cāhaṅkārastrividhatayā trividhakāryahetuḥ / taduktaṃ kaurme /

children.translated_text: The <s>vaikārika</s> (modified, sāttvic), the <s>taijasa</s> (luminous, rājasic), and the <s>bhūtādi</s> (origin of elements), which is <s>tāmasic</s>—
this threefold <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> arose from <s>Mahat</s>.
Thus. And that <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>, being threefold, is the cause of three kinds of effects. As stated in the <s>Kūrma Purāṇa</s>:
From the <s>taijasa</s> arise the sense organs; from the <s>vaikārika</s> arise the ten deities,
and <s>Manas</s> (mind), the eleventh, is here of dual nature by its own quality.

children.text:
bhūtatanmātrasargastu bhūtāderabhavan prajāḥ /
iti / vaikārikaḥ sāttvikaḥ / taijaso rājasaḥ / svaguṇenindriyavṛttiṣu sāhāyyarūpeṇotkarṣeṇa / ubhayātmakaṃ jñānakarmobhayendriyātmakam / anyatramanā abhūvaṃ nā 'śrauṣamityādiśrutyā manaso jñānakarmobhayendriyasahakāritvasiddheriti / ekādaśendriyadevāśca /
digvātārkapracetośvivahnīndropendramitrakāḥ /
candraśca
iti / ahaṅkāro nirūpitaḥ / indriyādīni nirūpyante / ahaṅkārādādau mana utpadyate /

children.translated_text: From the inclination toward sound, the ear of this contemplative being is born,
similarly the eye from the inclination toward form, and the nose from the desire to smell.

But the creation of elemental <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements)—from the <s>bhūtādi</s>, beings were produced. Thus: <s>vaikārika</s> means <s>sāttvika</s>; <s>taijasa</s> means <s>rājasa</s>. 'By its own quality' means by the excellence of its auxiliary role in the functions of the sense organs. 'Of dual nature' means having the nature of both knowledge-organs and action-organs. From the <s>Śruti</s>: 'My mind was elsewhere, I did not hear'—thus is established that <s>Manas</s> cooperates with both the organs of knowledge and action. The deities of the eleven organs are: <s>Dik</s> (space), <s>Vāta</s> (wind), <s>Arka</s> (sun), <s>Pracetas</s> (Varuṇa), the two <s>Aśvins</s>, <s>Vahni</s> (fire), <s>Indra</s>, <s>Upendra</s> (Viṣṇu), <s>Mitra</s>, and <s>Candra</s> (moon). Thus <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> has been examined. Now the sense organs and others are examined. From <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>, first <s>Manas</s> (mind) is produced.

children.text: ityādinā mokṣadharmādāvindriyādīnāṃ manovṛttirāgādikāryatvaśravaṇāt / tataścāhaṅkārāt saṅkalpapūrvakaṃ daśendriyāṇi pañcatanmātrāni cotpadyante / indriyatanmātrayośca kāryakāraṇabhāvasyābhāvāt kramaniyamo nāsti / tatrendriyeṣu nāstyavāntarakāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ pramāṇābhāvāt / tanmātreṣu tvasti / sa yathā / śabdatanmātrādvakṣyamāṇakrameṇa sparśatanmātraṃ śabdasparśobhayaguṇakamevaṃ krameṇaikaikaguṇavṛddhyā paratanmātratrayaṃ pūrvapūrvatanmātrebhya utpadyate pātañjalabhāṣye tanmātreṣu krameṇaikaikaguṇavṛddhivacanāt / tataśca pañcatanmātrebhyaḥ pañcabhūtāni jāyante / tatrāhaṅkārāt pañcatanmātrāṇāṃ taddvārā bhūtānāṃ cotpattau kramaḥ kūrmaviṣṇvādipurāṇeṣūktaḥ / yathā kūrme /

children.translated_text: The <s>bhūtādi</s> (origin of elements), undergoing modification, created the <s>śabda-tanmātra</s> (sound-subtle element),
and from that arose <s>ākāśa</s> (space), porous, characterized by sound.

Thus, from the <s>Mokṣadharma</s> and other texts, it is heard that the sense organs and others are effects of mental modifications such as desire. Therefore, from <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>, preceded by volition (<s>saṅkalpa</s>), the ten sense organs and five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) are produced. Since there is no cause-effect relationship between the sense organs and <s>tanmātras</s>, there is no fixed order between them. Among the sense organs themselves, there is no intermediate cause-effect relationship, due to the absence of evidence. But among the <s>tanmātras</s>, there is such a relationship. It is as follows: from the <s>śabda-tanmātra</s> (sound-subtle element), in the order to be described, the <s>sparśa-tanmātra</s> (touch-subtle element) arises possessing both sound and touch qualities; thus, in sequence, with each successive addition of one quality, the remaining three <s>tanmātras</s> are produced from the preceding ones—because in the <s>Pātañjala-bhāṣya</s> it is stated that among the <s>tanmātras</s> there is a successive increase of one quality each. Then from the five <s>tanmātras</s>, the five gross elements are born. The order of production of the five <s>tanmātras</s> from <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>, and through them the elements, is stated in the <s>Kūrma</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, and other <s>Purāṇas</s>. As in the <s>Kūrma Purāṇa</s>:
<s>Ākāśa</s>, undergoing modification, created the <s>sparśa-tanmātra</s> (touch-subtle element),

children.text: vāyurutpadyate tasmāt tasya sparśo guṇo mataḥ //
children.translated_text: and from that <s>Vāyu</s> (wind) is produced; touch is considered its quality.

children.text: ityādikrameṇeti / nanvevamākāśādibhūtacatuṣṭayasyāpi tattvāntarārambhakatvena prakṛtitvāpattyā kevalavikṛtitvasiddhāntakṣatiriti cenna / ākāśādīnāṃ sparśāditanmātreṣvahaṅkāropaṣṭambhamātreṇa kāraṇatvasya purāṇeṣūktatvāditi / tadevaṃ trayoviṃśatitattvānāmutpattiruktā / tatra pañcabhūtāni varjayitvā 'haṅkāraṃ ca buddhau praveśya saptadaśakaṃ liṅgaśarīrasañjñaṃ bhavati vahnerindhanavadātmano 'bhivyaktisthānatvāt / tacca sarvapuruṣāṇāṃ sargādāvutpadya prākṛtapralayaparyantaṃ tiṣṭhati / tenaiva cehalokaparalokayoḥ saṃsaraṇaṃ jīvānāṃ bhavati / prāṇaśca buddhereva vṛttibheda ityato na liṅgaśarīrāt pṛthaṅ nirdiśyate / tasya liṅgaśarīrasya sūkṣmāṇi pañcabhūtānyāśrayaścitrādivadāśrayaṃ vinā paramasūkṣmasya lokāntaragamanāsambhavāt / idaṃ ca liṅgaśarīramādau svayambhuva upādhibhūtamekameva jāyate / tasyaiva virāḍākhyavakṣyamāṇasthūlaśarīravat / tataśca vyaṣṭijīvānāmupādhibhūtāni vyaṣṭiliṅgaśarīrāṇi tadaṃśabhūtāni tato vibhajyante / piturliṅgaśarīrāt putraliṅgaśarīravat / taduktaṃ sūtrakāreṇa / vyaktibhedaḥ karmaviśeṣāditi / manunā 'pyuktam /

children.translated_text: Of those six elements of immeasurable power, their subtle parts
placing into the individual souls, he created all beings.

And so on in this order. Now, if the four elements beginning with <s>ākāśa</s> (space) also initiate other categories, would they not fall under the category of <s>prakṛti</s> (primal nature), thereby damaging the doctrine that they are merely modifications (<s>vikṛti</s>)? No, because the <s>Purāṇas</s> state that the causality of <s>ākāśa</s> and others with respect to the <s>tanmātras</s> of touch and so forth is merely through the support of <s>Ahaṅkāra</s>. Thus has been stated the origination of the twenty-three <s>tattvas</s> (principles). Among these, excluding the five gross elements and subsuming <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> within <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect), the group of seventeen is called the <s>liṅga-śarīra</s> (subtle body), because it is the locus of the self's manifestation, as fuel is for fire. This subtle body, for all <s>puruṣas</s> (souls), arises at the beginning of creation and persists until the dissolution into <s>Prakṛti</s>. Through it alone the transmigration of souls between this world and the next occurs. And <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) is merely a functional modification of <s>Buddhi</s>, and therefore is not mentioned separately from the <s>liṅga-śarīra</s>. The five subtle elements are the support of this <s>liṅga-śarīra</s>, like a canvas for a painting, because without a support the extremely subtle body could not travel to other worlds. This <s>liṅga-śarīra</s> is initially born as one single entity serving as the limiting adjunct of <s>Svayambhū</s> (the Self-born), just as its gross body is called <s>Virāṭ</s> (the Cosmic Form), to be described later. Then the individual subtle bodies, which serve as limiting adjuncts of individual souls, are portions of that and are divided from it, just as a son's subtle body comes from the father's subtle body. As stated by the author of the <s>Sūtras</s>: 'The differentiation of individuals is due to the difference of <s>karma</s>.' And <s>Manu</s> also says:

children.text: iti / ṣaṇṇāmiti ṣaḍindriyaṃ samastaliṅgaśarīropalakṣakam / tathā ca svayambhūḥ svaliṅgaśarīrāvayavān sūkṣmān alpān ātmamātrāsu svāṃśacetaneṣu saṃyojya sarvaprāṇinaḥ sasarjetyarthaḥ / liṅgaśarīraṃ nirūpitam / sthūlaśarīrotpattirucyate / daśaguṇitamahattattvamadhye 'haṅkāro 'haṅkārasyāpi daśaguṇitasya madhye vyoma vyomno 'pi daśaguṇitasya madhye vāyurvāyorapi daśaguṇitasya madhye tejaḥ tejaso 'pi daśaguṇitasya madhye jalaṃ jalasyāpi daśaguṇitasya madhye pṛthivī samutpadyate / saiva sthūlaśarīrasya bījam / tadeva ca pṛthivīrūpaṃ bījamaṇḍarūpeṇa pariṇamate / tasyāpi daśaguṇitasyāṇḍarūpasya pṛthivyāvaraṇasya madhye caturdaśabhuvanātmakaṃ svayambhuvaṃ sthūlaśarīraṃ tatsaṅkalpādevotpadyate / tenaiva śarīreṇa svayambhūrnārāyaṇa ityucyate / taduktaṃ manunā svayambhuvaṃ prakṛtya /

children.translated_text: He, desiring to create various beings, contemplating from his own body,
first created the waters, and in them he cast the seed.

Thus. 'Six' here refers to the six senses as a synecdoche for the entire <s>liṅga-śarīra</s> (subtle body). The meaning is that <s>Svayambhū</s> (the Self-born), joining subtle, small portions of his own <s>liṅga-śarīra</s> with the individual conscious beings who are his own parts, created all living beings. The <s>liṅga-śarīra</s> has been examined. Now the origin of the gross body (<s>sthūla-śarīra</s>) is described. Within the <s>Mahat-tattva</s> multiplied tenfold, <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> arises; within <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> also multiplied tenfold, space (<s>vyoman</s>); within space multiplied tenfold, wind (<s>vāyu</s>); within wind multiplied tenfold, fire (<s>tejas</s>); within fire multiplied tenfold, water (<s>jala</s>); within water multiplied tenfold, earth (<s>pṛthivī</s>) is produced. That itself is the seed of the gross body. And that seed in the form of earth transforms into the form of an egg (<s>aṇḍa</s>). Within the covering of earth in the form of that egg multiplied tenfold, the gross body of <s>Svayambhū</s>, consisting of fourteen worlds, is produced by his mere will. With that very body, <s>Svayambhū</s> is called <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>. As stated by <s>Manu</s>, referring to <s>Svayambhū</s>:
That seed became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun,
and in it was born <s>Brahmā</s> himself, the grandsire of all worlds.

children.text: sa vai śarīrī prathamaḥ sa vai puruṣa ucyate /
children.translated_text: He indeed is the first embodied being, he indeed is called <s>Puruṣa</s>,
he is the first creator of beings—<s>Brahmā</s> arose in the beginning.

children.text: āpe nārā iti proktā āpo vai narasūnavaḥ /
children.translated_text: The waters are called <s>nārā</s>, for the waters are indeed the offspring of <s>Nara</s> (the Cosmic Man);

children.text: tā yadasyāyanaṃ pūrvaṃ tena nārāyaṇaḥ smṛtaḥ //
children.translated_text: since they were his first abode (<s>ayana</s>), he is therefore known as <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>.

children.text: ityādineti / tata eva cādipuruṣāt vyaṣṭipuruṣāṇāṃ vibhāgādante ca tatraiva layāt sa eva caika ātmeti śrutismṛtyorvyavahriyate / ato na vyavahāraparatayā nārāyaṇa eva sarvabhūtānāmātmeti śrutismṛtivirodha iti / tataśca sa nārāyaṇo virāṭ śarīrī svanābhikamalakarṇikāsthānīyasya sumerorupari caturmukhākhyasvayambhuvaṃ sṛṣṭvā taddvārā 'nyānapi vyaṣṭiśarīriṇaḥ sthāvarāntān sasarja / tathā ca smaryate /

children.translated_text: From his body were produced those effects together with their instruments,
and the <s>kṣetrajñas</s> (knowers of the field, i.e., individual souls) were born from the limbs of that wise one.

And so on. Thus, because individual souls are differentiated from this very primordial <s>Puruṣa</s>, and at the end dissolve back into him, he alone is spoken of as the one <s>Ātman</s> (Self) in both <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>. Therefore, there is no contradiction of <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s> in the conventional statement that <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> alone is the <s>Ātman</s> of all beings. Then that <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, the embodied <s>Virāṭ</s> (Cosmic Form), having created <s>Svayambhū</s> called four-faced (<s>Caturmukha</s>, i.e., <s>Brahmā</s>) atop <s>Sumeru</s>, which occupies the position of the pericarp of the lotus of his own navel, through him created also the other individual embodied beings, down to immovable things. As it is remembered:

children.text: iti / yattu śeṣaśāyino nārāyaṇasya nābhikamalaśrotracakṣurādibhyaścaturmukhasyāvirbhāvaḥ śrūyate taddainandinasargeṣveva kalpabhedena mantavyam / dainandinapralayeṣveva hi nārāyaṇaśarīre praviśyaikībhūya suptānāṃ devānāṃ caturmukhādikrameṇāvirbhāvaḥ śeṣaśāyinaḥ sakāśādghaṭate na tvādisargeṣu / dainandinapralaya eva līlāvigraheṇa śayanāditi / tadevaṃ saṅkṣepataścaturviṃśatitattvāni teṣāṃ sṛṣṭirūpaṃ prayojanaṃ coktam / tatra yadyasmājjāyate tasya tadāpūraṇenaiva sthitiḥ tatastasya saṃhāro 'pi tatraiva bhavati /

children.translated_text: Whatever <s>tattva</s> (principle) is born from whatever, it dissolves back into that;
They dissolve in reverse order and arise successively one after another.

Thus. As for what is heard about the manifestation of the four-faced <s>Brahmā</s> from the navel-lotus, ears, eyes, and other organs of <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> who reclines on <s>Śeṣa</s>, that should be understood as occurring in daily creations with variations across <s>kalpas</s> (cosmic cycles). For it is only in daily dissolutions that the gods, having entered the body of <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> and become unified in sleep, can re-emerge in the order beginning with the four-faced one from the one reclining on <s>Śeṣa</s>, but not in the primordial creations. The reclining in a playful form occurs only during daily dissolution. Thus, in brief, the twenty-four <s>tattvas</s> (principles) and their creation-nature and purpose have been stated. Therein, whatever is born from whatever, its sustenance consists in being filled by that very thing, and hence its dissolution also occurs in that very thing.

children.text: iti bhāratādibhya iti / ete ca sṛṣṭisthitisaṃhārarūpāḥ sthūlā eva pariṇāmāścaturviṃśatitattvānāṃ kūṭasthapuruṣavivekāya pradarśitāḥ / sūkṣmā apyanye pratikṣaṇapariṇāmā eteṣāṃ smaryante / tathā /
nityadā hyaṅgabhūtāni bhavanti na bhavanti ca /
children.translated_text: For the constituent parts constantly come into being and cease to be,
But due to their subtlety, this is not perceived because of time's imperceptible velocity.

Thus from the <s>Bhārata</s> (Mahābhārata) and other texts. And these gross transformations in the form of creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the twenty-four <s>tattvas</s> (principles) have been shown for the purpose of discriminating the immutable <s>Puruṣa</s> (self). Other subtle moment-to-moment transformations of these are also mentioned in the tradition. As follows:

children.text: iti / ataśca sarvaṃ jaḍavastu paramārthataḥ sarvadaivāsaducyate / tataśca tasmādvirajyātmaiva paramārthasatyo duḥkhabhīrubhirdraṣṭavyaḥ / taduktamanugītāyām /

children.translated_text: Great is the tree whose seed originates from the <s>Avyakta</s> (unmanifest), whose trunk consists of <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect),
Whose branches are the great <s>Ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), and whose hollows sprout the <s>Indriyas</s> (senses),

Thus. And therefore, all insentient matter is ultimately said to be always unreal. And hence, the self which is detached from that alone is the ultimately real and should be contemplated by those who fear suffering. This has been stated in the <s>Anugītā</s>:
Whose major boughs are the <s>Mahābhūtas</s> (great elements), having sub-branches of the <s>Viśeṣas</s> (sense-particulars),
Ever-leaved, ever-blossoming, yielding both auspicious and inauspicious fruits,
The livelihood of all beings, rooted in <s>Brahman</s>, eternal.
Having known this in truth, with the supreme sword of knowledge,
Having cut it down and attained the imperishable state, one abandons birth and death.

children.text: iti śrīvijñānabhikṣuviracite sāṅkhyasāre vivekapratiyogināṃ prakṛtyādīnāṃ svarūpaparicchedaḥ // * //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the chapter on the essential nature of <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) and other counter-correlates of discrimination, in the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> composed by Śrī <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Thus ends the first part of the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s>.
Now begins the latter part.
First chapter.
Now, for the students to easily grasp through a garland of verses,
The self called <s>Puruṣa</s>, which is the correlate of discrimination, is described.
There, [the self] is generally established by the strength of the cognition 'I know';
As the witness, it is further proved by qualities such as eternality and pervasiveness.
The experiencer is eternal because all things exist for its sake and because they are produced by its <s>karma</s>,
This applies equally to all modifications beginning with <s>Mahat</s> (the great principle).
Moreover, because it is the substrate of unseen <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) in seed form,
And from the beginningless nature of the intellect and the rest, the beginninglessness of the experiencer is also established.
Without the beginningless relation of owned and owner, the status of experiencer cannot be established;
Ownership with respect to the <s>buddhis</s> (intellects) consists in possessing the <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) of the modifications belonging to one's own portion.
And mastership consists in the experiencer being the cause of modifications that produce impressions resting in itself;
Therefore, upon the destruction of ownership, <s>Kaivalya</s> (liberation) of the self is possible.
Since there can be no cause for the destruction of the beginningless nature of the experiencer,

children.text: na nāśo bhokturastīti bhoktā nityo hi sidhyati // ViSs_2,1.7 //
children.translated_text: There is no destruction of the experiencer — thus the experiencer is established as eternal.

children.text: janyo jñānaprakāśo 'sya nityatve tu na yujyate /
children.translated_text: If its consciousness-light were produced, then its eternality would not be fitting;
For nowhere is the arising of light observed in something that is inherently non-luminous.
In an effect, the quality called luminosity belongs to its constituent parts;

children.text: kāraṇaṃ tena nānityaḥ prakāśo nityavastuni // ViSs_2,1.9 //
children.translated_text: Therefore the light in an eternal substance is not non-eternal, because it is the cause.
Due to contact with the substrate of light, there is abundance of light in fuel,
And in a mirror, due to the removal of covering, there is the illusion of light arising.

children.text: tasmānnityātmano jñānaṃ nityaṃ vācyaṃ tathā sati /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the knowledge of the eternal self must be declared eternal; this being so,
By parsimony, knowledge itself is conceived as the self, without any substrate.
Being unsubstrated, it is considered a substance, and this is accepted because of conjunction and the like;
Therefore, cognitions such as 'I' are also appropriate with respect to knowledge.
The cognition 'I' with respect to the body is indeed fixed in the deluded, due to beginningless defect;

children.text: saṃyogāttatra piṇḍe tu jñānavattvamatiḥ pramā // ViSs_2,1.13 //
children.translated_text: But the cognition that the body possesses knowledge, due to conjunction, is a valid cognition.
Let there be cognitions of substratehood, smallness, birth, destruction, and the like;
These are like the cognitions of the ear in space — of object-knowledge in pure consciousness.
Therefore, by the reasoning of parsimony, and due to the absence of any contradicting evidence,
And through <s>Śruti</s> (scripture) and other authorities, the eternal self is established as being of the nature of consciousness alone.
That knowledge is all-pervading, due to its eternality and also because it pervades the body;

children.text: madhyatve nāśitā hi syādaṇutve vā 'lpadeśatā // ViSs_2,1.16 //
children.translated_text: If it were of medium size, destructibility would follow; or if atomic, limitation to a small space.
Even though all-pervading, because it is observed directly only through its own mental modifications,

children.text: na sarvatra sadā sarvabhānaṃ jñāne prasajyate // ViSs_2,1.17 //
children.translated_text: The objection of omniscience — awareness of everything everywhere always — does not arise regarding consciousness.
The awareness of objects in consciousness is regarded by the wise as a reflection of objects;
Only the mental modification has the fitness for direct reflection in consciousness.
Therefore, even in unattached, immutable, all-pervading, and steadfast consciousness,
The awareness of other things is considered to occur only through the medium of mental modifications, by the power of fruition.
Through positive and negative concomitance, all experience being produced by mental modifications,
Desire and the like reside in the intellects as their common locus, not in the selves.
Therefore, since each one's internal modifications rest in their own respective <s>buddhis</s> (intellects),

children.text: kūṭāstha eva sarvo 'pi cidākāśagaṇaḥ samaḥ // ViSs_2,1.21 //
children.translated_text: The entire host of consciousness-spaces is indeed immutable and equal.
Eternally pure, eternally awakened, eternally liberated, untainted,
Self-luminous, without substrate — a lamp unto all things.
But in that case, let there be oneness of selves for the sake of parsimony, just as in your own position;
'The difference of pleasure and pain, etc. is in the intellects alone' — if so objected, that is not valid.
Despite the group of consciousnesses being of one form, through the difference of experience and non-experience,
Mutual distinction is established as stated by <s>Śruti</s> (scripture) and <s>Smṛti</s> (tradition).
Even the experience of the self, consisting of reflections of pleasure and the like, is not ultimately real;

children.text: tathā 'pyasya citau bhāvābhāvau syātāṃ hi bhedakau // ViSs_2,1.25 //
children.translated_text: Nevertheless, the presence and absence of these in one's consciousness serve as differentiators.
Just as adventitious dark and colored hues differentiate crystals,
And your own analogy is incongruent, since the dissimilarity is not established in the case of space.
Thus ends the chapter on the essential nature of <s>Puruṣa</s> (the self), in the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> composed by Śrī <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Now the second chapter.
Now, regarding the difference between self and non-self, which consists of their respective merits and faults,

children.text: vakṣye vistārato yena viveko 'tisphuṭo bhavet // ViSs_2,2.1 //
children.translated_text: I shall speak at length, by which discrimination may become very clear.
In the dense space of universal selfhood, by powers set in motion through proximity,

children.text: jāyate līyate bhūtvā bhūyo 'yaṃ jagadambudaḥ // ViSs_2,2.2 //
children.translated_text: This cloud of the world arises, and having come into being, dissolves again and again.
Through the transformations of powers consisting of the three <s>guṇas</s>,  consciousness —
Is the material cause of the universe by way of being its substrate, without itself undergoing modification.
Just as water is considered the material cause of the earth by way of being its support,
So too consciousness is regarded as such through the medium of the earth-<s>tanmātra</s> (subtle element) resting within itself.
Therefore, <s>Brahman</s> is the material cause of the world even without undergoing modification;
It is called the ultimately real, synonymous with immutable and eternal.
Being ultimately real because it exists for its own sake and because it is established through self-experience;

children.text: svataḥ sthityā svataḥ siddhyā lokaiḥ sanniti hīryate // ViSs_2,2.6 //
children.translated_text: Through self-subsistence and self-establishment, it is accepted by people as truly existing.
Due to moment-to-moment transformation, and the passing away of each successive form,
All insentient reality beginning with <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) is unreal, like waves in the ocean.
But that which, even after the passage of time, does not acquire a different designation —
This is because the notion 'this is a thing' and the like arises from transformation.
And because its existence depends on another's purpose, and because it is established through another's perception,
It is considered to be existing only in dependence on another, neither truly existent on its own.

children.text: sato 'stitvaṃ tu nāsattā nāstitve satyatā kutaḥ /
children.translated_text: Of the real, there is existence but not non-existence; of the non-existent, how can there be reality?
Thus from the <s>Gāruḍa Purāṇa</s>; and thus is the determination of reality and unreality established.
Therefore, this world is neither real nor unreal, being of the nature of both real and unreal;
And because the cognition of it has the unreal as its object, that cognition is essentially an error.
Of the tree of the world, consciousness is the essence; the rest is without essence.
For the stable portion of the manifest world is consciousness alone, being without modification.
Everything other than that is declared to be worthless due to being without essence,
And likewise untrue and unreal, due to its instability compared to that consciousness.
Such is the reality of the self and the unreality of the non-self that has been shown,
As elaborated in the <s>Vāsiṣṭha</s> (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha) and other texts; a brief portion of that is stated here.
A dream is of unreal nature in the waking state; waking experience has an unreal form in the dream state.
Death is of unreal form during birth; birth too is of unreal nature during death.

children.text: jaganmayī bhrāntiriti na kadāpi na vidyate /
children.translated_text: The world-encompassing delusion neither ever does not exist,

children.text: vidyate na kadācicca jalabudbudavat sthitam // ViSs_2,2.16 //
children.translated_text: nor ever does exist — it is established like a water-bubble.
The self alone is the supreme reality; the other views of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) are not [real] —
like silver in a shell, like a desert mirage.
There exists the all-pervading, peaceful, dense mass of the supreme self, pure,
of inconceivable form consisting of consciousness alone, spread out as the supreme space.
That is all-pervading, all-powerful, everything, the self of all, itself —

children.text: yatra yatra yathodeti yathā '; 'ste tatra tatra vai // ViSs_2,2.19 //
children.translated_text: wherever and however it arises, and however it abides, there indeed.
The waves of the three worlds, consisting of appearance and disappearance,
flash and pass away in it, like mirages in a desert.
As if unreal yet real, like a moving wave in a stream of water,
like the splendor of a magic illusion of the mind, worldly existence is extended.
The universe is extended by <s>Brahmā</s>, by the mind of the Self-born alone;
therefore the visible universe is mind-made.

children.text: yo hyaśuddhamatirmūḍho rūḍho na vitate pade /
children.translated_text: For one of impure intellect, deluded, not established in the expanded state,
this world, though unreal, is as solid as a diamond.
Just as for one unskilled in gold, in a golden bracelet,
there is only the cognition of the bracelet, not the slightest awareness of gold,
so too for the ignorant, in this [world] shining with cities, houses, mountains, and great elephants,

children.text: iyaṃ dṛśyadṛgevāsti na tvanyā paramārthadṛk // ViSs_2,2.25 //
children.translated_text: there is only the vision of the visible, not the other — the ultimate vision.
By such statements in the <s>Vāsiṣṭha</s>, the absolute unreality of the world is not proclaimed;
for by other statements, the world as a pre-existing effect originating from <s>Prakṛti</s> is accepted.
That in which the world, divested of name and form, subsists —

children.text: tamāhuṃ prakṛtiṃ kecin māyāmeke 'pare tvaṇūn // ViSs_2,2.27 //
children.translated_text: some call it <s>Prakṛti</s>, some call it <s>Māyā</s> (illusion), and others call it atoms.
Just as [designs] rest within the belly of a stone in the state of deep sleep, like the lines of a lotus on a wheel-stone,
so too this series of the world rests within consciousness.
The creeper of <s>Prakṛti</s>, arisen in space, bearing the good fruit of the cosmic egg —
by such statements, due to the description of the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine of <s>satkārya</s> (pre-existing effect) and other doctrines.
Thus ends the chapter on the dissimilarity of the reality and unreality of the self and the non-self, in the <s>Sāṃkhyasāra</s> composed by <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Now the third chapter.
Thus the existence of the self, distinguished from other entities, has been shown;
now I shall describe its nature as consciousness (<s>cidrūpatā</s>), distinct from the modifications of the intellect.
<s>Anubhūti</s> (experience), <s>citi</s> (consciousness), <s>bodha</s> (awareness), <s>vedana</s> (knowing) — thus is <s>Puruṣa</s> called;
