the knowable, the inert, darkness, ignorance — thus are <s>Pradhāna</s> (the principal) and other entities called.
Knowing is called the knower only by virtue of its relation to the knowable,
just as light is called the illuminator only by virtue of its relation to the illuminable.
Or just as a perception, through the coloring by the object, becomes the illuminator of the object,
so too consciousness serves as the substratum of its own portion colored by the knowable.
In the unattached consciousness, this coloring by the knowable is not as in the intellects;

children.text: kintu sākṣāddvārato vā citi tatpratibimbanam // ViSs_2,3.5 //
children.translated_text: rather, it is the reflection of that in consciousness, either directly or through an intermediary.
External objects, due to the absence of the instrument called mental modification and due to non-coloring,

children.text: citirnaivekṣate cetyaṃ vibhutve 'pi ca sarvataḥ // ViSs_2,3.6 //
children.translated_text: consciousness does not perceive the perceivable, even though it is all-pervading everywhere.
Likewise, consciousness too, due to the absence of the instrument called mental modification,
like an object, except for the modification that is its own object, remains with unmanifested existence.
Thus consciousness, formless, of the nature of luminous space,
remains also in unmanifest form in <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) and such states, due to the absence of mental modifications.
But the modification of the intellect (<s>buddhi-vṛtti</s>) has form, is limited like a lamp,

children.text: vyaktā ca sarvadā tadvadasaṅkhyā kṣaṇabhaṅgurā // ViSs_2,3.9 //
children.translated_text: is always manifest, and likewise is innumerable and momentary.
And it is considered inert because it is an object for another, like a pot or lamp;
but the luminosity of the modification is unimpaired because it takes the form of the object.
Just as a mirror, because of its fitness to take the form of objects, illuminates them,
so too the modification, because of its fitness to take all forms, illuminates all.
However, consciousness is not the seer of the modification as something separate from it;
for there would be the fault of complexity in attributing knowership to both.
But another object superimposed on the intellect, reflected through that modification,
is perceived by experience alone — no other entity such as the intellect is the seer of all.
Thus the distinctness of consciousness from the modifications of the intellect has been stated;
this dissimilarity called the difference between consciousness and non-consciousness is clearly evident from the body and other entities.
Through the mutual reflection giving rise to similarity between modification and consciousness,
the designation of consciousness is applied to the modification, like the designation of fire to heated iron.
This discrimination between modification and consciousness is not possible for one of limited intellect;

children.text: tārkikā yatra sammūḍhāḥ sāṅkhyānāṃ śreṣṭhatā yataḥ // ViSs_2,3.16 //
children.translated_text: the logicians (<s>Tārkikas</s>) are bewildered here, which is why the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> hold supremacy.
The <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (idealist) Buddhists, due to non-discrimination between modification and consciousness,

children.text: jñātātmatvaśrutau mūḍhā menire kṣaṇikāṃ citim // ViSs_2,3.17 //
children.translated_text: being confused by the <s>Śruti</s> statement that the self has the nature of a knower, considered consciousness to be momentary.
This discrimination between <s>sattva</s> (intellect) and <s>Puruṣa</s>, that is, between modification and its illumination,
is not impossible for the wise — just as for swans, the discrimination between milk and water.
<s>Saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) ends with this, and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) is established precisely in this —
namely, the ascertainment of that consciousness through discrimination from modifications.
Everyone knows experience, but no one knows its true nature as knowing;
for even though it shines, it requires discrimination alone.

children.text: ātmā vivektuṃ bāhyārthe na śakyo vṛtimiśraṇāt /
children.translated_text: The self cannot be discriminated in external objects due to mixture with modifications;

children.text: ato vṛttau vivektavyo vṛttibodhatayaiva saḥ // ViSs_2,3.21 //
children.translated_text: therefore it should be discriminated in the modification itself, as the illumination of the modification.
Just as fire cannot be discriminated by the intellect due to its mixture with coal,

children.text: so 'ṅgāre tu vivekārho kāṣṭhadagdhṛtayā sphuṭam // ViSs_2,3.22 //
children.translated_text: but in the coal it can clearly be discriminated as the burner of wood —
therefore in <s>Śruti</s>, through the discrimination of the seen modification in dream,
the seer of that modification is shown in its nature as self-luminous.

children.text: sākṣāt prakāśo yo yasya sa tadbhinno mato budhaiḥ /
children.translated_text: That which directly illuminates something is considered by the wise as different from it —
just as light from pots etc., and modifications too from the light of consciousness.
Because it directly illuminates the modification, therefore the self, whose nature is experience,

children.text: vṛttibhyo bhinna ātmeti śīghro mārgaḥ svadarśane // ViSs_2,3.25 //
children.translated_text: is different from modifications — this is the swift path to self-realization.
In such manner, through the distinctness from the luminosity of <s>buddhi-sattva</s> (the purity of the intellect),
the light of consciousness (<s>cit-prakāśa</s>) is established as the illuminator of it.
Therefore, through examples such as the dream body etc., as shown by <s>Śruti</s> and other texts,
consciousness is considered as distinct from the body, senses, and objects of the waking state.

children.text: svapne dehādikaṃ sarvaṃ cidbhinnaṃ citi bhāsate /
children.translated_text: In dream, the body and all else, being different from consciousness, shine in consciousness;
in waking it is the same, with the distinction that external objects also shine.
In dream, because of being mind-made, everything is directly an object of consciousness;

children.text: karaṇadvārato bāhyaṃ cito jāgrati gocaraḥ // ViSs_2,3.29 //
children.translated_text: in waking, external objects are objects of consciousness through instruments.
Everything — body and all else — in both dream and waking, in one form,
shines in the space of consciousness; here there is no difference due to the distinction of objects as external or internal.
In the space of consciousness, the intellect, taking the form of objects either from latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) or from valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) —

children.text: tataścito 'rthabhānaṃ yat tat samaṃ svapnajāgratoḥ // ViSs_2,3.31 //
children.translated_text: therefore, the shining of objects in consciousness is the same in both dream and waking.
This is proclaimed through direct personal experience alone, not indirectly;
there is no means equal to the dream analogy for self-realization.
Just as in deep sleep and dream, one perceives everything in one's own self alone,

children.text: ātmānaṃ caikadeśasthaṃ manyate jāgare tathā // ViSs_2,3.33 //
children.translated_text: so too in waking one considers oneself as situated in a particular place.
Deep sleep is the true nature of the self, because then it abides in its own nature;

children.text: jāgratsvapnau māyikau tu mṛṣāsārūpyato dhiyā // ViSs_2,3.34 //
children.translated_text: waking and dream are illusory, because the intellect falsely assumes similarity.
The deep sleep of the intellect is the obscuration by <s>tamas</s> (darkness); distinct from that,
the deep sleep of consciousness is the absence of the veil called the visible, namely mental modifications.
Full, immutable, and eternal, the seer only of its own respective mental modifications —
due to the absence of the visible called modifications, <s>Puruṣa</s> does not perceive at all times.
Just as consciousness exists where there is modification, so too everywhere and always;
the deluded vainly grieve over the destruction, decay, and such of the self.
The intellect, which dwells in the body, the cause of the great disease of the experience of suffering,
is not abandoned by the deluded, because the happiness of the great sleep of ignorance is dear to them.
If the beginningless householder-life of attachment to the intellect is not abandoned through discrimination,
there is no liberation through mere external renunciation — there is only supreme suffering here and hereafter.
In all selves, one's own and others', which are of the uniform nature of consciousness alone,
the distinction of self and other etc. is false, being merely a discrimination pertaining to the intellect.
Superimposing agency upon the self onto the master who is pure consciousness and without qualities,
the intellect is destroyed by its own actions through the offense of disregarding the master.

children.text: sādhvī tu dhīḥ patiṃ dṛṣṭvā yāthātathyena tatparā /
children.translated_text: But the virtuous intellect, seeing the master as he truly is, devoted to him,

children.text: ihānandamayī cānte patidehe layaṃ vrajet // ViSs_2,3.42 //
children.translated_text: becomes full of bliss here, and at the end dissolves into the body of the master.
'I am not the doer, not happy, not sorrowful—I am of the nature of pure consciousness like space'—

children.text: evaṃ nāthaṃ cintayantī na patyurduḥkhabhogadā // ViSs_2,3.43 //
children.translated_text: thus contemplating the lord, the intellect does not inflict the experience of suffering upon the master.
Thus ends the chapter on the distinction between the consciousness and unconsciousness of the self and non-self, in the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> composed by Śrī <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Thus has been described the self's distinction from the intellect and others—
its nature as the light of consciousness; now likewise its nature as bliss will be described.
Suffering is the expectation of desired pleasure; happiness is the transcendence of both suffering and pleasure—
thus according to <s>Smṛti</s>, the blissful nature of the self consists in its being eternally free from suffering.
The overriding of conventional meaning by technical definition is universally accepted;
otherwise this technical definition in the science of liberation would be meaningless.
Alternatively, through indirect expression, for the attainment of supreme dearness,

children.text: rūpikā sukhagīḥ puṃsi vibhutvāptyai svaśabdavat // ViSs_2,4.4 //
children.translated_text: the figurative description of bliss in <s>Puruṣa</s> is for attaining all-pervasiveness, like the word 'sva' (own).
From the <s>Śruti</s> texts such as 'neither bliss nor absence of bliss,' it is clear
that the denial of the nature of bliss in the self is accompanied by reasoning.
Similarly, from the <s>Śruti</s> 'not this, not this' (<s>neti neti</s>), since it is devoid of any object of meditation,
the established position is that the negative statement is stronger than the positive statement.
'Without the absence of bliss' declares the enjoyership of bliss through one's own limiting adjuncts—

children.text: svāmitvarūpiṇīṃ vakti na nirdhana itīva hi // ViSs_2,4.7 //
children.translated_text: indicating mastership, just like the expression 'not without wealth.'
By the <s>Śruti</s> 'dearer than everything else,' the self is declared

children.text: ukta ātmā priyastasya sukhatvoktiśca nocitā // ViSs_2,4.8 //
children.translated_text: to be dear, even more than pleasure; the attribution of pleasure-nature to it is not appropriate.
From the <s>Vedānta-sūtra</s>, 'bliss and others belong to <s>Pradhāna</s>'—

children.text: vedānte 'pi na siddhānta ātmanaḥ sukharūpatā // ViSs_2,4.9 //
children.translated_text: even in <s>Vedānta</s>, the doctrine that the self has the nature of pleasure is not established.
This has been examined by us at length in the <s>Brahma-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya</s>;
the non-pleasure nature of consciousness having been established, love (<s>premā</s>) is now explained.
'May I not cease to be; may I always exist'—this is the metaphorical expression of

children.text: nirnimitto 'nurāgo yaḥ sa premā paramaściti // ViSs_2,4.11 //
children.translated_text: the causeless affection which is the supreme love in consciousness.
Since the intellect has no remainder of anything else, this affection is not even for pleasures;

children.text: ataḥ priyatamaḥ svātmā nānyo 'to hyadhikaḥ priyaḥ // ViSs_2,4.12 //
children.translated_text: therefore one's own self is the dearest—there is nothing dearer than it.
Love in the self, by virtue of selfhood, does not depend on pleasure and the like;

children.text: ahaṃ syāmiti cedyasmāt sukhaṃ syāmiti neṣyate // ViSs_2,4.13 //
children.translated_text: for the desire 'may I be' is not the same as 'may I be happy.'
Thus, whether happiness, absence of suffering, or selfhood—

children.text: premṇi prayojikā siddhā svataḥpremātmataiva tu // ViSs_2,4.14 //
children.translated_text: it is established that what motivates love is selfhood itself, for love of self is self-existent.
Therefore, in reality, the self alone is dear, not anything conditioned or other;
love for conditioned and other things, being unstable, is not ultimately real.
Delight in other things such as pleasures is impermanent, due to lack of discrimination and the like;

children.text: ātmaprītistu nityā 'to nityānandaḥ pumān mataḥ // ViSs_2,4.16 //
children.translated_text: but delight in the self is eternal—therefore <s>Puruṣa</s> is regarded as eternally blissful.
If the concentrated intellect were to perceive the dearness of the self—

children.text: sarvātiśāyinīṃ tarhi sukhābdhau kiṃ na majjati // ViSs_2,4.17 //
children.translated_text: surpassing all else—would it not then be immersed in an ocean of bliss?
In the world, happiness is seen to arise from the intellect's perception of what is dear;
therefore, supreme happiness may be inferred from the vision of what is supremely dear.
Since all love everywhere is for the sake of the self, the self is inherently dear;
thus the eternal <s>Śruti</s> declares, with the intent of prescribing the vision of the self.
From the vision of the beloved self, know that incomparable happiness arises;

children.text: bhuñjate tat sukhaṃ dhīrā jīvanmuktā mahādhiyaḥ // ViSs_2,4.20 //
children.translated_text: the steadfast ones, liberated while living (<s>jīvanmukta</s>), of great wisdom, enjoy that happiness.
The inner bliss of the self is real and unfailing for the <s>yogin</s>;

children.text: apaśyan kṛpaṇo bāhyasukhārthī vañcito janaḥ // ViSs_2,4.21 //
children.translated_text: the miserable person who does not see it, seeking external pleasures, is deceived.
The embodied being, hoping for happiness, looking outward through the apertures of the senses,

children.text: vātāyanairgṛhītvā 'ntaḥ sukhaṃ vetti na bāhyadṛk // ViSs_2,4.22 //
children.translated_text: through these windows grasping inward, knows happiness—but not the one whose vision is only external.
Obtained through suffering, consisting of suffering, causing great suffering in their consequences—
fie upon those semblances of pleasure arising from sense objects, which obstruct the bliss of one's own self!
Thus ends the chapter on the distinction between the dearness and non-dearness of the self and non-self, in the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> composed by Śrī <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Through three chapters has been described the nature of <s>saccidānanda</s> (existence-consciousness-bliss)—
the threefold characteristic of the self, celebrated in <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>.
The opposite of these has been clearly set forth as the characteristic of all else;

children.text: ābhyāṃ tu guṇadoṣābhyāṃ viveko doṣahṛt paraḥ // ViSs_2,5.2 //
children.translated_text: and through these merits and faults, discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) is the supreme remover of defects.
Other distinctions also, such as qualitylessness versus possession of qualities,

children.text: bahūni vakṣye saṅkṣepāt pumprakṛtyorataḥ param // ViSs_2,5.3 //
children.translated_text: many I shall state briefly hereafter regarding <s>Puruṣa</s> and <s>Prakṛti</s>.
Since pleasure and other qualities are produced by the modification of the intellect taking the form of objects,
they are attributed to the self through co-reference (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>), for the sake of simplicity.
Since <s>Mahat</s> and others are insentient, their cause too is regarded as insentient;

children.text: kāryakāraṇasājātyaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ loke hi sarvataḥ // ViSs_2,5.5 //
children.translated_text: for the homogeneity of cause and effect is observed everywhere in the world.
Therefore the self is established as pure consciousness alone, by the principle of parsimony;
all qualities belong to <s>Prakṛti</s>, and all other modifications likewise.

children.text: ātmā tu nirguṇastadvat kūṭasthaśca mato budhaiḥ /
children.translated_text: But the self is without qualities, and likewise is regarded by the wise as immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>);

children.text: citeḥ kūṭasthasañjñā tu sthiratvād girikūṭavat // ViSs_2,5.7 //
children.translated_text: consciousness is called <s>kūṭastha</s> because of its steadfastness, like the peak of a mountain.
Staining, in association with what is other, is the coloring by the forms of those things;
just as <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impressions) arise in the intellect from contact with objects.
And from the contact of substances with vessels and the like, the impressions of those substances remain;

children.text: lepahetuśca sambandhaḥ saṅgaḥ sambandhi cāñjanam // ViSs_2,5.9 //
children.translated_text: the cause of staining is association; attachment (<s>saṅga</s>) is the connection, and collyrium (<s>añjana</s>) is the coloring agent.
Therefore <s>Puruṣa</s> is said to be unstained (<s>nirañjana</s>), unattached (<s>asaṅga</s>), and without blemish (<s>nirlepa</s>),
illustrated by the great sages with examples such as space and the lotus leaf.
In the ocean of infinite power that is pure consciousness, stirred by the wind of <s>Puruṣa</s>'s purpose,
the powers of <s>sattva</s> and others take on the form of the bubbles of the universe.
Therefore the lord is consciousness itself; by its mere proximity to the world,
it serves as the impeller of insentient things, like a magnet impels pieces of iron.
<s>Puruṣa</s> alone is the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, the lord of all,
because the insentient group functions for the sake of the master, like servants for their lord of death.
The instruments in the bodies, like officials acting for the king,
naturally present the class of enjoyable objects to the mind, which is the minister.
The intellect reports the self endowed with those enjoyables to consciousness;
by mere observation, the self, the lord of all, enjoys them, like a king.
The body is the master of wealth and the like; the sense organ is the master of the body;
the intellect is the master of the sense organ; and the self is the supreme master of the intellect.
Since there is no other impeller of the immutable lord,
as the ultimate limit of lordship, the seer is indeed the supreme lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>).
The lordship of others is adventitious and encumbered by many activities;
but the lordship of the self, being without activity, is faultless and beginningless.
For the self is replete with all powers, performing the cosmic dance of the circle of powers;

children.text: saṃsāraṃ tannivṛttiṃ ca māyayā '; 'pnoti helayā // ViSs_2,5.19 //
children.translated_text: through <s>Māyā</s>, it effortlessly brings about both <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) and its cessation.
This lordship of the self, surpassing all and faultless—
for the <s>yogin</s> who perceives it, even the lordship of <s>Brahmā</s> seems like a blade of grass.
The body is said to be the self of external things; the senses are the self of the body;
the intellect is the self of the internal sense realm; and the self of the intellect is consciousness, like space.
Therefore, as the ultimate limit of selfhood, consciousness is called <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self);
and through conjunction with the inner instruments (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), consciousness is called <s>Jīva</s> (individual soul).
Free from the effects of ignorance—thus is the <s>Smṛti</s> regarding <s>Paramātman</s>;

children.text: yasya yadvyāpakaṃ tasya tadbrahmā 'to dharādikam // ViSs_2,5.23 //
children.translated_text: whatever pervades anything is its <s>Brahman</s>; hence earth and the rest—
up to <s>Prakṛti</s>, each is <s>Brahman</s> relative to its own effects;
even in the theistic <s>Sāṅkhya</s> doctrine, this is attributed to consciousness alone.

children.text: pare vā paramātmatvādikaṃ tu na jaḍe kvacit /
children.translated_text: Or in the supreme reality—but attributes like supreme selfhood are never in the insentient;

children.text: adhyakṣavyāpakatvābhyāṃ paraṃ brahma tu cetanaḥ // ViSs_2,5.25 //
children.translated_text: the supreme <s>Brahman</s> is the conscious being, by virtue of being the overseer and pervader.

children.text: tasyādhyakṣaṃ vyāpakaṃ ca na hetuvidhayā 'sti hi /
children.translated_text: Its overseeing and pervading are not in the manner of a cause, indeed;
the innumerable selves, like portions of space, are of one undivided nature.
Therefore it is called a mass of consciousness (<s>cidghana</s>), a mass of knowledge (<s>vijñānaghana</s>), a mass of self (<s>ātmaghana</s>);
because its luminosity is self-dependent, and because it is its own seer.
The <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self) has been stated to be self-luminous; the others [i.e., the non-Self categories] are different from it.

children.text: bhogo 'bhyavahṛtiḥ sā ca kūṭasthe nāsti dhīṣviva // ViSs_2,5.28 //
children.translated_text: Experience (<s>bhoga</s>) is [direct] consumption, and that does not exist in the immutable one (<s>kūṭastha</s>), just as [it does not exist] in cognitions themselves.
But the enjoyership consists of secondary experience called the reflection in mental modifications (<s>dhīvṛtti</s>);
since he directly witnesses the mental modifications, the <s>Puruṣa</s> is called the witness of <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect).

children.text: vinā vikāraṃ draṣṭṛtvāt sākṣī tūkto 'khilasya saḥ /
children.translated_text: Because he sees without undergoing modification, he is called the witness (<s>sākṣin</s>) of everything;
since the witnesshood is of the nature of the coloring by objects of consciousness (<s>caitya</s>), the witnesshood of consciousness is also impermanent.
This [designation of witness] is merely indicative, [given] to distinguish [the Self] from the insentient.
Therefore the <s>Puruṣa</s> is said to be indescribable, atomic, and subtle.
Because it is invisible without a visible [object], it is also called <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest), though it exists.
The invisible <s>Rāhu</s> is perceived through the seized moon; likewise,
the invisible face [is seen] in a mirror—so too consciousness (<s>cit</s>) [is known] through one's own <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect).

children.text: citi viśvasya saṅgaśced viśvaṃ bhāseta sarvadā // ViSs_2,5.33 //
children.translated_text: If there were contact of the universe with consciousness, the universe would always be illumined.
Therefore, although consciousness is the support of the universe, it is proclaimed as void, like space;
the deluded intellect, superimposing the defects of the visible upon the pure [consciousness],
suffers by seeing defects as if there were impurity in space, like [seeing dirt] in a mirror.

children.text: vastutaściti nāstyeva malo dṛśyāśritaḥ sadā // ViSs_2,5.35 //
children.translated_text: In reality, in consciousness there is absolutely no impurity; [impurity] always resides in the visible [objects].
Therefore the <s>Puruṣa</s> is said to be pure, self-abiding, and faultless;
since there is no difference characterized by dissimilarity among those of the same class,

children.text: ata ātmā samaḥ prokta aikarūpyācca sarvadā /
children.translated_text: therefore the Self is said to be equal [in all beings] and always of one form.
Being the superintendent of the body, [he is called] embodied (<s>dehin</s>); through manifestation in the city [of the body], the <s>Puruṣa</s> [is so named].
Being alone, without a second, he is also called <s>kevala</s> (absolute).
Because the power of consciousness is unobstructed, the <s>Puruṣa</s> is said to be uncovered.
Being the master of all, the Self is [called] <s>kṣetrajña</s> (knower of the field) because of knowing the field;
sporting in the petal-like modifications of the lotus of intellect in the lake of the heart,
as if moving about, enjoying the fish of bliss, he is called <s>Haṃsa</s> (the Swan).

children.text: hakāreṇa bahiryāti sakāreṇa viśan punaḥ // ViSs_2,5.40 //
children.translated_text: By the syllable 'ha' he goes out, and by the syllable 'sa' he enters again;
through the function of <s>prāṇa</s> (exhalation) and <s>apāna</s> (inhalation) as well, the Self of living beings is called <s>Haṃsa</s>.
In the cave of the inner chamber of the heart, within the house that is the body, with <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect) as his wife,
being manifested together with her, as if sleeping, he dwells in the cave.
By his mere proximity, causing the transformation of his own <s>Māyā</s> (illusion) consisting of the three <s>guṇas</s>,
the Self is called <s>Māyin</s> (the Illusionist), wearing the false garb created by that [<s>Māyā</s>].

children.text: svānyekādaśa bhūtāni pañcaitāni tu ṣoḍaśa // ViSs_2,5.43 //
children.translated_text: His own eleven [organs] and five elements—these sixteen
are called the parts (<s>kalās</s>) of the <s>Puruṣa</s>, but in reality, being partless, he is <s>niṣkala</s> (without parts).

children.text: ahaṃśabdaḥ svāmivācī svāmī sākṣī tu cetasaḥ // ViSs_2,5.44 //
children.translated_text: The word 'I' (<s>aham</s>) denotes the master, and the master is the witness of the mind;
therefore by the word 'I,' pure consciousness alone is denoted by the wise.
The lord of all, the knower of all, the doer of all, non-dual—such is the <s>Puruṣa</s>;
just as a king is called the lord of all men in a general sense,
so the non-duality of the Self is described by the <s>Sūtras</s> merely in terms of class [similarity].
For at the time of dissolution, [there is] the absence of duality with anything of a different class for the Selves.
Due to non-attachment, [he is] eternally pure; and due to being of the nature of consciousness, eternally awakened;
likewise eternally liberated—the <s>Puruṣa</s> is considered [thus] due to being eternally free from suffering.
Thus, in the direction indicated by the <s>Guru</s> and the <s>śāstras</s> (scriptures), and through one's own experience,
let the wise accomplish the discrimination of Self from non-Self through [recognizing] their dissimilarity.
Through these four chapters, the dissimilarity between <s>Puruṣa</s> and <s>Prakṛti</s> has been stated in great detail;
this collection of distinguishing attributes bestows swift liberation upon meditators.
Thus ends the chapter on the collection of distinguishing attributes of the Self, in the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> composed by Śrī <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Now, the Sixth Chapter.
Having understood discrimination through sound reasoning, it is [then] directly experienced;

children.text: rājayogaṃ yathā kuryāt samāsena taducyate // ViSs_2,6.1 //
children.translated_text: how one should practice <s>Rāja Yoga</s>—that is stated here in brief.
One who is incapable of <s>Rāja Yoga</s> is qualified for <s>Haṭha Yoga</s>.
And in the <s>Vāsiṣṭha</s> [Rāmāyaṇa], thus was spoken by <s>Bhusuṇḍa</s> to <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>:
'In <s>Rāja Yoga</s>, the principal [means] are knowledge and mental activity; in <s>Haṭha Yoga</s>, <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control) and <s>āsana</s> (posture);'
'these principal [means] serve as auxiliaries to each other, and should be practiced according to one's capacity.'
The infinite defects in sense objects that are declared in <s>Śruti</s> and <s>Smṛti</s>,
those should first be contemplated by <s>yogins</s> for the steadiness of mind.
The innumerable seeds of desire that sprout in the heart,
in that [heart] resembling a dense forest, the crop of knowledge and merit does not grow.
But when the seeds of desire in the mind have been burned by the fire of seeing defects [in sense objects],
and [the mind] has been plowed by the [teachings of] <s>Guru</s> and <s>śāstras</s>, in that good field [the crop of knowledge] flourishes.
Seeing abundant non-existence in [seemingly] existing things, and unpleasantness in [seemingly] pleasant ones,

children.text: sukheṣu pracuraṃ duḥkhaṃ paśyan dhīro virajyate // ViSs_2,6.7 //
children.translated_text: and abundant suffering in [seeming] pleasures, the wise one becomes dispassionate.
Even the world of <s>Brahmā</s> is a hell, [being subject to] destruction and filled with impurity;
and being joined with others superior to oneself, it is afflicted with suffering due to the three <s>guṇas</s>.
Even by those dwelling there, efforts are made for liberation, by those who fear [re]birth.

children.text: ato jñeyaḥ samāsena lokaḥ sarvo 'pi duḥkhayukt // ViSs_2,6.9 //
children.translated_text: Therefore it should be known, in brief, that every world is accompanied by suffering.

children.text: idaṃ me syādidaṃ mā syāditīcchāvyathitaṃ manaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'May this be mine, may this not be mine'—the mind tormented by such desires;

children.text: svabhāvāt tena vijñeyaṃ duḥkhaṃ cittena saṅgatiḥ // ViSs_2,6.10 //
children.translated_text: by its very nature, association with the mind should be known as suffering.
The supreme happiness is deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>); the experience of sense objects is suffering—
this is the summary of pleasure and pain; what need is there for much more discourse?
Therefore, having examined sense objects as appearing [desirable but] truly harmful,
the wise seeker of the highest truth should abandon them, like snakes that seem delightful to children.
Thus, through seeing the infinite defects [in sense objects] and the like, for the attenuation of attachment,
one should always meditate upon the pure Self through discrimination from <s>Māyā</s> (illusion).

children.text: idaṃ taditi nirdeṣṭuṃ guruṇā 'pi na śakyate /
children.translated_text: It cannot be pointed out as 'this' or 'that' even by the <s>Guru</s>;
to one who is detached, the truth of the Self (<s>ātmatattva</s>) reveals itself of its own accord.
Of the nature of the illumination of <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect), the witness of <s>Buddhi</s>, beyond <s>Buddhi</s>, all-pervading,
immutable—'I am the sun of consciousness'—thus one should meditate with one-pointed concentration.
The awareness through mental modifications appears small and perishable, like the space inside a pot;
'in reality, I, the awareness [behind] modifications, am complete and imperishable, like [infinite] space.'
All that is seen within is called a modification of <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect);

children.text: tebhyo duḥkhātmakebhyo 'haṃ sākṣāt tadvīkṣitā pṛthak // ViSs_2,6.17 //
children.translated_text: 'from those [modifications], which are of the nature of suffering, I am separate—I am their direct witness.'
For there would be a contradiction between object and agent if a modification were to illuminate [another] modification,
and in positing a stream of modifications [illuminating each other], there would be undue complexity—thus it is established.
Joy, grief, fear, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and likewise
aversion, conceit, wretchedness, sleep, laziness, passion, and the like—
filled with merit and demerit, this <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect) is full of suffering, [belonging] to me [only apparently];
it merely reveals the Self, just as the sick [are revealed to] the sun [which remains unaffected].
'I am all-pervading, peaceful, a mass of supreme Self-nature, pure,'
'inconceivable, a sky of pure consciousness alone, a mirror of the universe, imperishable,'
'untainted, without support, without qualities, without affliction,'
'without distinction from those of the same class, the illuminator of all objects.'
'<s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Maheśa</s>, and the rest, down to immovable beings—all conscious beings,'
'are non-different from me in their essential Self-nature, due to the absence of dissimilarity'—thus one should meditate.
'I and the other <s>Puruṣas</s> are of the form of the same sky of consciousness;'

children.text: ata ātmaika evā 'hamiti śrutiṣu gīyate // ViSs_2,6.24 //
children.translated_text: 'therefore "the Self alone is one" is proclaimed in the <s>Śrutis</s>.'

children.text: iti paśyan svabhogaiśca yogī viśvaṃ prapūjayet /
children.translated_text: Seeing thus, the <s>yogin</s> should worship the entire universe with his own enjoyments.
This <s>ātmayoga</s> (union with the Self) is declared by <s>Śruti</s> for <s>Sāṅkhya</s> practitioners.
'Seeing the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self,'
'seeing equally, the worshiper of the Self attains sovereignty (<s>svārājya</s>).'
Thus by <s>Manu</s> also, the worship of the Self is declared as a limb of knowledge.
Therefore, through the gift of fearlessness and worship with one's own enjoyments and the like,
honoring all beings, one should meditate upon the Self.
[When one sees that] even the enjoyment of <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Śiva</s>, and the rest is [transient], attachment diminishes;
therefore, through seeing one's equality with them, the <s>yogin</s> should contemplate equality.

children.text: utpattau pralaye caiva sarvāvasthāsu sarvadā // ViSs_2,6.29 //
children.translated_text: In creation, in dissolution, and in all states at all times,
the oneness of form of all [Selves] as seers [is the same]—whence then attachment and the like?

children.text: viṣṇvādayo mahaiśvaryaṃ bhuñja nā api nādhikā // ViSs_2,6.30 //
children.translated_text: <s>Viṣṇu</s> and the rest, even while enjoying great lordship, are not superior [in their essential nature];
'therefore enough with those lordships dear to the undiscriminating, [which are not superior] to me.'
'Seeing something as superior to oneself through qualities, actions, and the like—'

children.text: tadarthaṃ yatate loko nāhaṃ paśyāmi me 'dhikam /
children.translated_text: 'for that the world strives; but I do not see anything superior to myself.'

children.text: tathā nyūnaṃ na paśyāmi yadatikramaśaṅkayā // ViSs_2,6.32 //
children.translated_text: 'Likewise I see nothing inferior, through fear of transgression from which'
'like gods [striving] for the conquest of demons, I shall strive with the intention of conquering that [false perception of inequality].'

children.text: ahaṃ yathā tathaivānye ābrahmā nārakā janāḥ // ViSs_2,6.33 //
children.translated_text: As I am, so too are all other beings, from <s>Brahmā</s> down to those in hell.
They are seen with love as one's own self, like father, brother, son, and the rest.

children.text: ka īśa īśitavyo vā kaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ ko 'dhamo 'pi vā // ViSs_2,6.34 //
children.translated_text: Who is the lord, or who is to be ruled? Who is superior, or who is inferior?
The <s>Śruti</s> says: 'From perceiving difference in what is undivided, there comes the fear of death.'
In the space of consciousness, which is of one nature, the appearances of lord and non-lord etc.
are entirely unreal, like the appearance of various colors in a crystal.

children.text: dhiyāṃ rūpaiḥ pumāneko bahurūpa iveyate // ViSs_2,6.36 //
children.translated_text: Through the forms of intellects, the one <s>Puruṣa</s> appears as if of many forms,
like a magician bearing many forms through the appearances of wolf-skin and other disguises.
Embracing me who am formless, she who bears diverse forms—
<s>Māyā</s> alone, the one who dances, deludes all intellects.
The difference among souls is due to difference in intellects, like the difference in reflections of the sun in different waters.
And the difference in space through the form of openings is due to differences in pots etc.

children.text: ataḥ śuddho buddhamuktaḥ sarvadā sarvago 'vyayaḥ // ViSs_2,6.39 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, the Self is pure, awakened, liberated, always all-pervading, and imperishable.
'I,' 'others,' and 'alas!'—the notions of enemy, friend, and so on are false.
In <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Īśa</s>, <s>Hara</s>, <s>Indra</s>, and in all groups of beings likewise,
the division into superior, inferior, and middling is false, produced by <s>Māyā</s>.
Because of the threefold nature of <s>Māyā</s> consisting of the three <s>guṇas</s>, even of the Self
the threefold division of superior, inferior, and middling does not exist in its own nature.
As in the body, so elsewhere—this imperishable light of consciousness
has only the difference of being manifest or unmanifest, internally and externally.
Thus other <s>Puruṣas</s> too, without distinction of bound and liberated,
and without distinction of lord and non-lord—therefore there is no purpose of life for me.

children.text: mahānidraiva me sādhvī duḥkhabhogaharā priyā // ViSs_2,6.44 //
children.translated_text: The great sleep alone is my faithful wife, the beloved who removes the experience of suffering—
disliked by those of deluded minds, unfaithful for those whose selves are seized by intellect.

children.text: cidādarśe mayi dhiyo yadyapi pratibimbanam // ViSs_2,6.45 //
children.translated_text: Although intellects are reflected in me, the mirror of consciousness,

children.text: tattvato naiva doṣāya tathā 'pi tyājyameva tat /
children.translated_text: in truth that is not a defect; yet even so, it should be abandoned.

children.text: svabhāvādasya heyatvaṃ svānubhūtyā hi sidhyati // ViSs_2,6.46 //
children.translated_text: That its rejectability is by its own nature is established through one's own experience.

children.text: yathā ko 'pi parasyāpi vairūpyaṃ na didṛkṣati /
children.translated_text: Just as no one wishes to see deformity, even in another,
this faithful wife, projecting her own defects onto her lord, grieves.

children.text: nirdoṣaṃ svāminaṃ dṛṣṭvā nirdoṣā syāt pativratā /
children.translated_text: Seeing her lord to be without fault, the devoted wife becomes faultless.
Thus, even amidst her various forms, I am always of one form.
Whether enjoying or not enjoying her who exists for my sake and goes to no other,
just as a mirror retains one form in states of association and dissociation with limiting adjuncts—oh!
of a pure mirror, a mercury-backed mirror that is mine—
the defects belonging to the seen and the intellect do not exist in the direct seer, the Lord.

children.text: na santi mayi mohādyā bhāskare bhāsyadoṣavat /
children.translated_text: In me there are no delusion etc., like the defects of the illuminated objects do not exist in the sun.
The intellect, bound by sufferings, having abandoned its own self and having attained my nature,

children.text: mucyate duḥkhabandhāddhīrna me mokṣo na bandhanam /
children.translated_text: is freed from the bondage of suffering—for me there is neither liberation nor bondage.
In the immutable, unattached, conscious space, the reflection of the intellect's suffering—

children.text: yo 'nyo bandho bhogarūpaḥ so 'pi ciddarpaṇe mṛṣā /
children.translated_text: whatever other bondage exists in the form of experience, that too is false in the mirror of consciousness.
The witness of the three states beginning with waking, yet free from them,
I am complete, the sun of consciousness, without rising or setting.

children.text: darpaṇe mukhavadviśvaṃ mayi bodhe na tāttvikam // ViSs_2,6.54 //
children.translated_text: Like a face in a mirror, the universe in me, in awareness, is not real.
And regarding all-pervasiveness, internally and externally, from the non-perception in deep sleep etc.,

children.text: mayi vā 'nyatra vā puṃsi kevalānubhave vibhau // ViSs_2,6.55 //
children.translated_text: whether in me or in another soul, in the all-pervading one of pure experience—
what appears is a transformation, being of the nature of a reflection in intellect.

children.text: śuktau rajatavad viśvamato mayi na doṣakṛt // ViSs_2,6.56 //
children.translated_text: Like silver in a shell, the universe therefore does not produce defect in me.
Like water in a mirage, likewise like a city etc. in the sky.

children.text: kālatraye 'pi nāstyeva mayi viśvaṃ sanātane // ViSs_2,6.57 //
children.translated_text: In all three times the universe does not exist in me, the eternal one.

children.text: anyatrāstvathavā mā 'stu buddhyādau mama tena kim /
children.translated_text: Whether it exists elsewhere or not, in <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect) etc.—what is that to me?

children.text: mayi sarvaṃ yathā vyomni sarvatrāhaṃ yathā nabhaḥ // ViSs_2,6.58 //
children.translated_text: Everything is in me as in space; I am everywhere, like the sky.

children.text: na sarvaṃ mayi sarvatra nāhaṃ cālepataḥ khavat /
children.translated_text: Yet not everything is in me, nor am I everywhere, from the standpoint of non-attachment, like space.
Therefore, by the non-difference called non-separation, like milk and water,
the great sages sing that this universe is of the nature of consciousness.
The world is mine because it exists for my sake, like my body's pleasure etc.

children.text: yatha mama tathā 'nyeṣāṃ mamaiveti dhiyo bhramaḥ /
children.translated_text: As it is mine, so too for others—the notion 'mine alone' is a delusion of the intellect.

children.text: vastutastu na kasyāpi kimapi vyabhicārataḥ // ViSs_2,6.61 //
children.translated_text: In reality, nothing belongs to anyone, due to the transience of ownership,
because of the impermanence of ownership, like a traveler's lodging house.

children.text: ekaṃ cinmātramastīha śuddhaṃ śūnyaṃ nirañjanam // ViSs_2,6.62 //
children.translated_text: There exists here only one pure consciousness, pure, void, untainted—

children.text: sūkṣmāt sūkṣmataraṃ tatra na jaganna jagatkriyā /
children.translated_text: subtler than the subtle. In that, there is no world, nor worldly activity.
What is seen is the succession of each one's own intellects, rich with all visible objects,
reflected in the great mirror of the orb of consciousness.

children.text: kvacidvyaktaṃ kvacit sūkṣmaṃ nabhaḥ sarvatra tiṣṭhati // ViSs_2,6.64 //
children.translated_text: Just as space exists everywhere, sometimes manifest, sometimes subtle,

children.text: yathā tathā cidākāśaṃ dhīdeśe 'nyatra ca sthitam /
children.translated_text: so too the space of consciousness abides in the region of intellect and elsewhere.
The universe is made of the space of consciousness; hence wherever the intellect moves,
wherever it wanders, it shines right there, like a pot etc. in sunlight.
<s>Dharma</s> (virtue) and <s>adharma</s> (vice), birth and death, pleasure and pain, and all the rest—

children.text: jāgratyapi mṛṣā svapna iva janmādikaṃ mama /
children.translated_text: even in waking, birth etc. are unreal for me, as in a dream.
The notion of birth and destruction of consciousness arises from association and dissociation with the visible,
In the great sleep, the streams of existence, birth, death,
and bad dreams are momentary intellects;
I behold them, unsmeared in form—
what are dense, clustered, or departed clouds to the sun?
like the apparent defects of manifestation and non-manifestation of the moon.
Thus, meditating constantly in this manner with a focused mind, the wise one
directly realizes the truth of the Self, which is beyond the reach of speech.

children.text: svarūpaṃ nirmalaṃ śāntaṃ manastyajati cet kṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: If the mind abandons the pure, peaceful essential nature even for a moment,
at that very moment, due to residual impressions of the visible, the senses become agitated.
Those enemies that are the senses, whether arisen or not yet arisen,
one should slay again and again with the thunderbolt of discrimination alone, as <s>Indra</s> slays mountains.
Thus ends the chapter on the method of <s>Rāja Yoga</s> in the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> composed by Śrī <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The characteristics of a <s>jīvanmukta</s> (one liberated while living) who thus experiences the Self—
I shall clearly describe them, by which the examination of knowledge and ignorance may be made.
Through hearing, reflection, or otherwise, due to the delusion of self-knowledge,
one who is unlearned may render even a teacher ignorant; and one may be ignorant though considering oneself a knower.
Supernatural powers, knowledge of the future, and the like are not the marks of true knowledge,
for liberation even without these has been stated by the author of the <s>Yoga Bhāṣya</s>.
The Vedic and <s>Smṛti</s> statements regarding the knower who partakes of liberation—
only the indicative ones are written down, indeed for the increase of faith.
'Where all beings have become the very Self of the one who knows—

children.text: tatra ko mohaḥ kaḥ śoka ekatvamanupaśyataḥ // ViSs_2,7.5 //
children.translated_text: what delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?'
'He who is without attachment everywhere, upon obtaining this or that, good or bad,

children.text: nābhinandanti na dveṣṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā // ViSs_2,7.6 //
children.translated_text: neither rejoices nor hates—his wisdom is firmly established.'

children.text: na vismarati sarvatra yathā satatago gatim /
children.translated_text: Just as one who constantly walks does not forget the path anywhere,

children.text: na vismarati niścetyaṃ cinmātraṃ prājñadhīstathā // ViSs_2,7.7 //
children.translated_text: so the intellect of the wise one does not forget pure consciousness, the object of certainty.
The radiance of whose face neither rises nor sets in pleasure or pain,
whose condition remains as before—he is called a <s>jīvanmukta</s> (one liberated while living).

children.text: yo jāgartti suṣuptastho yasya jāgranna vidyate /
children.translated_text: He who remains awake while situated in deep sleep, for whom waking does not exist,

children.text: yasya nirvāsano bodhaḥ sa jīvanmukta ucyate // ViSs_2,7.9 //
children.translated_text: whose awakening is free from impressions—he is called a <s>jīvanmukta</s>.
Even while acting in accordance with passion, aversion, fear, and the like,
he who is internally transparent like space—he is called a <s>jīvanmukta</s>.

children.text: yasya nāhaṅkṛto bhāvo buddhiryasya na lipyate /
children.translated_text: He whose nature is free from ego, whose intellect is not tainted,

children.text: kurvato 'kurvato vā 'pi sa jīvanmukta ucyate // ViSs_2,7.11 //
children.translated_text: whether acting or not acting—he is called a <s>jīvanmukta</s>.
Even if the sun were cool-rayed, even if the orb of the moon were exceedingly hot,
even if fire were to burn downward—the <s>jīvanmukta</s> would not think otherwise.
'These powers of the conscious Self ever manifest here'—
in such a web of wonders, no curiosity arises in him.
Just as a woman devoted to another man, though busy with household work,
savors internally the elixir of the company of her beloved,

children.text: evaṃ tattve pare śuddhe dhīro viśrāntimāgataḥ /
children.translated_text: so the wise one who has found repose in the supreme, pure reality,
savors that very thing internally, even while engaging in external affairs.
He who is always absorbed in the Self, always inward-turned and happy—
Deep and serene, like a great lake in a mountain.
Stirred by the nectar of supreme bliss, he rejoices in himself by himself;
Having renounced all actions, ever joyful, free from affliction.

children.text: na puṇyena na pāpena netareṇāpi lipyate /
children.translated_text: He is not tainted by merit, nor by sin, nor by anything else;

children.text: yena kena cidācchanno yena kena cidāśitaḥ // ViSs_2,7.18 //
children.translated_text: Covered by whatever garment, eating whatever food,

children.text: yatra kvacana śāyī ca sa samrāḍiva rājate /
children.translated_text: Sleeping wherever he may be, he shines like an emperor.
Beyond what is prescribed by the codes of <s>varṇa</s> (caste), <s>dharma</s>, <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life), conduct, scripture, <s>mantras</s>, and reasoning,
He emerges from the snare of the world like a lion from a cage.
Beyond the range of words, incomparable, having seen through the desires for sense-objects as insubstantial,
He has attained an indescribable splendor, like the autumnal sky.
Without hymns of praise, without salutations, free from the worship of those worthy of worship;
This alone is truly the sign of one whose form is beyond signs,
Who has found contentment through the cessation of the long-wandering delusion of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence):
That in whom lust, anger, sorrow, greed,
Delusion, and calamities daily diminish with precision.
Whether united with or separated from the course of righteous conduct and rules.
For one who is endowed with rest in the <s>Turīya</s> (fourth state), who has turned back from the ocean of worldly existence,
He has no concern with what is done or undone, nor with the bewilderments of <s>Śruti</s> (scripture) and <s>Smṛti</s> (tradition).

children.text: tanuṃ tayajatu vā tīrthe śvapacasya gṛhe 'thavā /
children.translated_text: Let him abandon the body at a sacred pilgrimage site or in the house of a <s>śvapaca</s> (outcaste);
At the time of attaining knowledge, one of pure mind is indeed liberated.

children.text: na mokṣo nabhasaḥ pṛṣṭhe na pātāle na bhūtale /
children.translated_text: <s>Mokṣa</s> (liberation) is not on the surface of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor on the earth;

children.text: sarvāśāsaṅkṣaye cetaḥkṣayo mokṣa iti śruteḥ // ViSs_2,7.25 //
children.translated_text: Liberation is the dissolution of the mind upon the complete cessation of all desires — so says the scripture.
Having relinquished the state of <s>Jīvanmukti</s> (liberation while living), when one's body is claimed by time,
One enters bodiless liberation, as wind enters into stillness.
Just as in a mirror that has not received any reflection of mountains and the like,
There would be mere mirror-ness, consisting solely of its own nature —
When the delusion of the seen — 'I,' 'you,' 'the world,' and so forth — has subsided,

children.text: syāt tādṛśī kevalatā sthite draṣṭaryavīkṣaṇe // ViSs_2,7.28 //
children.translated_text: Such aloneness prevails, with the seer remaining in non-seeing.
Pure consciousness, devoid of objects of thought, infinite, ageless, auspicious,
Without beginning, middle, or end, free from affliction, free from disease.

children.text: na śūnyaṃ nāpi cākāraṃ na dṛśyaṃ na ca darśanam /
children.translated_text: It is neither void nor with form, neither the seen nor the seeing;
Indescribable, unmanifest — that Something remains.
Thus ends the chapter on <s>Jīvanmukti</s> (liberation while living) and <s>Parama Mukti</s> (supreme liberation), in the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> composed by Śrī <s>Vijñānabhikṣu</s>.
Thus ends the latter part of the <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s>.
The treatise called <s>Sāṅkhyasāra</s> is completed.
